title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues and Diagonalization
Definition: An eigenvector of a matrix \(A\) is a nonzero vector \(\mathbf{v}\) such that
\[
A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}
\] for some scalar \(\lambda\), called the eigenvalue corresponding to \(\mathbf{v}\).
Spectral Decomposition: A matrix \(A\) is diagonalizable if it can be written as
\[
A = V \Lambda V^{-1},
\] where the columns of \(V\) are the eigenvectors of \(A\) and \(\Lambda\) is a diagonal matrix containing the corresponding eigenvalues.
NB1: Not all matrices are diagonalizable. In such cases, we may need to consider generalized eigenvectors and the Jordan canonical form.
NB2: When \(A\) is symmetric, it is always diagonalizable with an orthonormal set of eigenvectors.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Why Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues Matter
Variational Interpretation:Eigenvectors and eigenvalues are solutions of optimization problems:
\[
\lambda_{\max}(A) = \max_{\mathbf{v} \neq 0} \frac{\mathbf{v}^\top A \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{v}}
\]
This can be generalized to other eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors (see the Courant-Fischer min-max theorem in review notes).
Geometric Interpretation: Eigenvectors indicate directions in which the linear transformation associated with the matrix acts by simply scaling, and the corresponding eigenvalues indicate the scaling factor.
For a symmetric matrix \(A\): \[
A = Q \Lambda Q^\top = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{q}_i \mathbf{q}_i^\top,
\] a weighted sum of projections onto the eigenvectors.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Why Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues Matter 2
Variational Interpretation:Eigenvectors and eigenvalues are solutions of optimization problems.
Geometric Interpretation: Eigenvectors indicate directions in which the linear transformation associated with the matrix acts by simply scaling, and the corresponding eigenvalues indicate the scaling factor.
Algebraic Interpretation: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues provide a way to understand the structure of a matrix through its diagonalization, revealing invariant subspaces and simplifying matrix computations.
\[
A^t \mathbf{u} = Q \lambda^t Q^{-1} \mathbf{u}
\] This is super-useful for solving linear ODEs: \[
\mathbf{\dot{x}}(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t) \to
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \mathbf{x}(0) = Q e^{\Lambda t} Q^{-1} \mathbf{x}(0).
\]

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
A random surfer
Web = directed graph \(G=(V,E)\). The surfer follows a random out-link, but with probability \(1-\alpha\) teleports to a uniformly random page:
\[
M \;=\; \alpha P + (1-\alpha)\,\tfrac1n \mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top .
\]

The PageRank vector is a left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1:
\[
\pi^\top M = \pi^\top .
\]


Perron–Frobenius: \(M\) is strictly positive and stochastic, so \(\pi\) exists, is unique, and is entrywise positive.

§1 total ~12 min. Perron–Frobenius (informal): strictly positive irreducible matrix ⇒ real, simple, largest-modulus eigenvalue with positive eigenvector.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: The algorithm is the eigenvector computation
text:
The algorithm is the eigenvector computation
Power iteration: \(\;\pi_{k+1}^\top = \pi_k^\top M\).

Why it converges: teleportation is a contraction in \(\ell_1\). A difference of probability vectors sums to \(0\), so the teleport term drops out:
\[
\|\pi_{k+1} - \pi\|_1 = \alpha\,\big\|(\pi_k - \pi)^\top P\big\|_1 \;\le\; \alpha\,\|\pi_k - \pi\|_1,\\
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \|\pi_k - \pi\|_1 \le 2\,\alpha^k .
\]
Spectrally: \[\;\operatorname{spec}(M) = \{1\} \cup \alpha\cdot\{\lambda_2(P),\dots,\lambda_n(P)\},\] so the spectral gap is \(1 - |\lambda_2(M)| \ge 1 - \alpha\).



Discussion: what does a small spectral gap mean physically for the surfer?


Answer: slow mixing — the surfer’s distribution takes a long time to forget where it started. Same phenomenon as Markov chain mixing time; formalized with graph spectral gaps in a few weeks.
Contraction proof: for probability vectors \(x,y\), \(z = x-y\) has \(z^\top\mathbf 1 = 0\), so \(z^\top M = \alpha z^\top P + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{n}(z^\top\mathbf 1)\mathbf 1^\top = \alpha z^\top P\); \(P\) row-stochastic gives \(\|z^\top P\|_1 \le \|z\|_1\). Apply with \(x = \pi_k\), \(y = \pi\).
Eigenvalue proof (Haveliwala–Kamvar 2003): if \(x^\top M = \lambda x^\top\) with \(\lambda \ne 1\), then \(M\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\) forces \(x^\top\mathbf 1 = 0\), hence \(x^\top P = (\lambda/\alpha)x^\top\), so \(|\lambda| \le \alpha\). Equality iff \(P\) has a second unimodular eigenvalue (e.g. two closed components). Assumes dangling pages are patched so \(P\) is row-stochastic.
Why prefer the contraction: \(M\) is non-normal, so the eigenvalue bound only gives \(C|\lambda_2(M)|^k\) with \(C\) depending on eigenvector conditioning; the \(\ell_1\) argument has constant 1 and holds for every \(k\). That is the dashed \(\alpha^k\) line in the demo. Well-mixed graph: \(|\lambda_2(P)|\) small, so the error beats \(\alpha^k\) by a lot; two communities: \(\lambda_2(P) \approx 1\), error tracks \(\alpha^k\).

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: A remark to flag now, pay off later
text:
A remark to flag now, pay off later
\(M\) comes from a directed graph, so it is generally

not symmetric,
not even normal (\(MM^* \neq M^*M\)),
with left and right eigenvectors that differ.

No inner product makes it self-adjoint: no diagonal reweighting enforces detailed balance on a generic directed graph.

Perron–Frobenius still gives a real, positive dominant eigenvalue — but the clean orthogonal-eigenbasis picture of the spectral theorem is not operating here.


Hold that thought — it resurfaces in §2, in reverse.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Partitioning a graph
Weighted undirected graph, adjacency \(A\), degrees \(D\), Laplacian
\[
L = D - A, \qquad x^\top L x = \sum_{(i,j)\in E} w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2 \;\ge 0, \qquad L\mathbf 1 = 0 .
\]

Goal: clusters with few crossing edges (Conductance/Normalized Cut Objective). NP-hard as stated.


Relax the \(\pm1\) indicator to any real vector:
\[
\min_{\mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf 1 = 0}\; \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top L \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^\top D \mathbf{x}} \;=\; \lambda_2(L),
\]
attained exactly by the Fiedler vector \(v_2\).

§2 total ~15 min. The Rayleigh quotient on the board: extrema over the unit sphere are the extreme eigenvalues; Courant–Fischer gives the rest.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Self-adjointness, precisely
For any undirected weighted graph (no regularity needed):

\(L_{rw} = D^{-1}L\) and \(P = D^{-1}A\) are self-adjoint w.r.t. \(\langle x,y\rangle_D = x^\top D y\) — this is exactly detailed balance for \(\pi \propto \deg\);
\(\mathcal L = D^{1/2} L_{rw} D^{-1/2}\) is the same operator, self-adjoint w.r.t. the standard inner product.



A change of which inner product you measure against — not a repair of a broken operator. Undirected graphs get this for free; directed graphs (§1) generally do not.


This is Exercise 4 in the Linear Algebra Review note — assign before or after this lecture.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
An eigenvalue certifies a bottleneck
Conductance of \(G\): \[
h(G) = \min_{S}\; \frac{|\partial S|}{\min\big(\mathrm{vol}(S),\, \mathrm{vol}(V\setminus S)\big)} .
\]

Cheeger’s inequality. With \(\lambda_2\) the second-smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathcal L\),
\[
\frac{\lambda_2}{2} \;\le\; h(G) \;\le\; \sqrt{2\lambda_2} .
\]



Not a heuristic: a two-sided, provable certificate.
The upper bound is constructive: a sweep cut of \(D^{-1/2}v_2\) achieves it (the dashed line in the demo).
Proof later in the term; then SDP relaxations (ARV) and sparsification (Spielman–Teng).


~10 min. Goal today is the shape of the result, not the proof. Fill in the week number for the proof.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
The spectral theorem
PCA computes eigenvectors of the (symmetric, PSD) covariance matrix. Time to state what §2–3 were quietly leaning on:

Spectral theorem. If \(A = A^*\) on an \(n\)-dimensional inner product space, there is an orthonormal basis \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues: \[A = Q\Lambda Q^*, \qquad Q \text{ unitary}.\]


SVD is the rectangular generalization: \(A = U\Sigma V^*\).
Eckart–Young. \(A_k = \sum_{i\le k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^*\) is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in Frobenius and operator norm: \(\;\|A - A_k\|_F^2 = \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 .\)

§4 total ~12 min. This is the result every student has used via sklearn without knowing it’s a spectral-theorem statement dressed up.

text:
The framing line

“Every example so far that behaved nicely — orthogonal eigenvectors, real eigenvalues, stable numerics — was secretly symmetric, or could be made symmetric. PageRank’s matrix was not, and we saw the clean picture partially break. Much of this course is about knowing which case you’re in before you start computing.”

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Heat on a graph
\[
\frac{du}{dt} = -Lu,\quad u(0)=u_0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
u(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\langle u_0, v_k\rangle\, v_k .
\]


\(\lambda_1 = 0\): the constant mode survives forever (equilibrium).
Every other mode decays at its own rate \(e^{-\lambda_k t}\).
The slowest non-constant mode is \(v_2\) — the Fiedler vector again.




Same eigenvector, two jobs: “the best 2-way cut” and “the last non-uniform heat left before equilibrium.”


§5 total ~12–15 min. Loosely follows the opening of Rosenberg, The Laplacian on a Riemannian Manifold. Qualitative today.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Demo: watching heat diffuse
open in new tab ↗



Cycle first: press Play; the blue curve is the continuous heat kernel on a circle of the same length (Fourier eigenbasis) — discrete and continuous agree once the high modes are gone. Then “Two clusters + bridge”: after the high modes die, what remains is exactly the orange Fiedler mode — one cluster warm, the other cool. Path: slowest of all (λ₂ ≈ π²/n²).

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
From graphs to manifolds
Replace the graph by a compact Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\) and \(L\) by the Laplace–Beltrami operator \(\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}\):

self-adjoint, \(\Delta \succeq 0\), discrete spectrum \(0 = \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty\);
eigenfunctions \(\phi_k\) form an orthonormal basis of \(L^2(M)\).


Heat equation \(\partial_t u = -\Delta u\), solved by the heat kernel
\[
K(t,x,y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\phi_k(x)\,\phi_k(y).
\]
The same equation as the graph case — a finite sum becomes a discrete-but-infinite one.

The eigenbasis comes from Theorem 7.1 in Linear Algebra Review, Part II (see its Section 8), applied to the compact self-adjoint resolvent (I+Δ)⁻¹.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Where the geometry hides
Heat trace, as \(t \to 0^+\) (Minakshisundaram–Pleijel):
\[
Z(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t} \;\sim\; (4\pi t)^{-n/2}\Big(\mathrm{Vol}(M) + \tfrac{t}{6}\!\int_M \mathrm{Scal}\,dV + O(t^2)\Big).
\]
From the list of eigenvalues alone you read off:

the dimension \(n\) (rate of blow-up),
the volume (leading coefficient),
the total scalar curvature (next coefficient).


Weyl’s law, from the other end: \[N(\lambda) = \#\{k: \lambda_k \le \lambda\} \;\sim\; \frac{\omega_n \mathrm{Vol}(M)}{(2\pi)^n}\,\lambda^{n/2}.\]

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: Can one hear the shape of a drum?
text:
Can one hear the shape of a drum?


Kac (1966): a drum’s shape determines its frequencies. Can you run that backward?

Gordon–Webb–Wolpert (1992): no. Two non-isometric planar drums with identical spectra.



The spectrum determines a great deal (dimension, volume, curvature, bottlenecks, …) — but not everything. Where exactly the line falls is a theme we return to.



Either way, actually computing with a continuous operator like \(\Delta\) is a real numerical problem. →

“Spectral” for eigenvalue problems comes from the analogy with spectral lines in physics.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Same word, different community
Solve \(\;u'' = e^{4x}\) on \([-1,1]\), \(\;u(\pm1)=0\).

Finite differences: local stencils, error \(O(N^{-2})\).
Chebyshev collocation: global polynomial basis, error \(O(\rho^{-N})\) for smooth \(u\) — “spectral” convergence.



§6 ~15 min. The intended “wow”: ~20 Chebyshev points reach machine precision; finite differences with thousands of points are still around 1e-6. Mention Orr–Sommerfeld (next slide) as a name-drop.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Planting a seed: non-normal operators
The Orr–Sommerfeld operator (hydrodynamic stability) is not self-adjoint.

Eigenvalues alone can badly mislead about its behavior.
Transient growth, sensitivity to perturbation → pseudospectra.


Same warning as PageRank, now for differential operators. We return to this once we have the machinery.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: Spherical harmonics and the global forecast
text:
Spherical harmonics and the global forecast
Operational global forecasting has long used the spectral transform method: expand fields in spherical harmonics (eigenfunctions of \(\Delta\) on \(S^2\)).

Smooth global fields ⇒ exponential convergence (as in §6).
A modest number of degrees of freedom buys enormous accuracy.


Not a classroom curiosity: part of why a global forecast is computationally tractable at all.


~5 min. Currency check before lecture: confirm current operational models’ numerics before citing specifics (e.g. ECMWF IFS), since this has been an active area of change.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Roadmap for the semester

Spectral graph theory proper: expanders, mixing times, Cheeger’s inequality (proved).
Spectral algorithms in ML: clustering, embeddings, low-rank models, diffusion maps.
The recurring question underneath all of it:


What do we actually need — self-adjointness, normality, or just diagonalizability — and what breaks when we don’t have it?

PageRank and directed graphs were today’s first data point. More will come.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Operators and the spectral theorem
Inner product / adjoint. On \(\mathbb F^n\), \(\langle x,y\rangle = y^*x\). The adjoint satisfies \(\langle Ax,y\rangle = \langle x,A^*y\rangle\). \(A\) is self-adjoint if \(A=A^*\); normal if \(AA^* = A^*A\) (orthonormal eigenbasis, possibly complex eigenvalues).
Spectral theorem. \(A=A^*\) on an \(n\)-dim inner product space ⇒ orthonormal eigenbasis, real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n\); \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\).
Rayleigh quotient. \(R_A(x) = \langle Ax,x\rangle / \langle x,x\rangle\); extrema on the unit sphere are the extreme eigenvalues (Courant–Fischer gives the rest).
Perron–Frobenius (informal). Strictly positive irreducible matrix ⇒ real, simple, largest-in-modulus eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector.
SVD / Eckart–Young. \(A = U\Sigma V^*\); \(A_k = \sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i u_i v_i^*\) is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in Frobenius and operator norm.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Graphs
For \(G=(V,E,w)\) undirected, symmetric adjacency \(A\), \(D = \mathrm{diag}(\deg)\):

\(L = D - A\): symmetric, PSD, \(\mathbf 1\in\ker L\).
\(L_{rw} = D^{-1}L\), \(\;P = D^{-1}A\).
\(\mathcal L = D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2} = I - D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\).

Degree-weighted inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle_D = x^\top D y\): \(L_{rw}\) and \(P\) are self-adjoint w.r.t. it; \(\mathcal L = D^{1/2}L_{rw}D^{-1/2}\) is self-adjoint w.r.t. the standard one.
Conductance \(h(G) = \min_S |\partial S| / \min(\mathrm{vol}(S),\mathrm{vol}(V\setminus S))\). Cheeger: \(\lambda_2(\mathcal L)/2 \le h(G) \le \sqrt{2\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}\).
Heat semigroup. \(u(t) = e^{-tL}u_0 = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle u_0,v_k\rangle v_k\); kernel \(K_t = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}v_kv_k^\top\).

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Manifolds and numerics
Laplace–Beltrami. On compact \((M,g)\), \(\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}\) is self-adjoint, \(\Delta\succeq0\), spectrum \(0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\cdots\to\infty\), eigenfunctions \(\phi_k\) an ONB of \(L^2(M)\). Heat kernel \(K(t,x,y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y)\).
Heat trace. \(Z(t) = \operatorname{Tr} e^{-t\Delta} \sim (4\pi t)^{-n/2}\big(\mathrm{Vol}(M) + \tfrac t6\int_M \mathrm{Scal}\,dV + O(t^2)\big)\).
Weyl’s law. \(N(\lambda) \sim \dfrac{\omega_n\mathrm{Vol}(M)}{(2\pi)^n}\lambda^{n/2}\).
Spectral convergence. For smooth data, global (Chebyshev/Fourier) bases converge faster than any power of \(1/N\); local finite-difference stencils converge at a fixed polynomial rate.

title: Exercise: The Perron–Frobenius Theorem
text:
In class we used the Perron–Frobenius Theorem on the random-walk matrix \(P = D^{-1}A\) of a connected graph \(G\). \(P\) is row-stochastic, and the theorem, applied to \(P^\top\), gives eigenvalue \(1\) with a positive left eigenvector \(\pi\), so that \(\pi^\top P = \pi^\top\). Normalized, \(\pi\) is the stationary distribution of the random walk. In this exercise you will prove a version of the Perron–Frobenius Theorem for irreducible non-negative matrices.
Prove the following theorem.
Theorem. Let \(M\) be an \(n \times n\) non-negative matrix that is irreducible: for all \(i, j \in [n]\) there is a positive integer \(k\) such that \((M^k)_{ij} \neq 0\). Then there is a real number \(\lambda\) such that:

(a) \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(M\);
(b) every other eigenvalue \(\mu\) of \(M\) satisfies \(|\mu| \le \lambda\);
(c) \(\lambda\) has an eigenvector \(x\) that is entrywise positive;
(d) every non-negative eigenvector of \(M\), for any eigenvalue, is a scalar multiple of \(x\).

Convince yourself that you can view an irreducible non-negative matrix as the adjacency matrix of a directed graph that is strongly connected. The graph may have self-loops. Strongly connected means there is a directed path from every vertex \(i\) to every other vertex \(j\).

Hint 1. Call a non-negative, nonzero vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^n\) \(\rho\)-good if \((Mx)_i \ge \rho\, x_i\) for all \(i \in [n]\). Consider the largest \(\rho\) for which some \(\rho\)-good vector exists. Suppose \(x\) is \(\rho\)-good but not an eigenvector. Show how to use \(x\) to build a vector \(y\) that is \((\rho + \epsilon)\)-good for some \(\epsilon > 0\). This is a contradiction. Remember to use the irreducibility of \(M\).
Hint 2. Let \(\rho\) be the largest value for which a \(\rho\)-good vector exists. Among the \(\rho\)-good vectors, pick an \(x\) with the fewest coordinates \(i\) such that \((Mx)_i = \rho\, x_i\), and call this set of coordinates \(S_x\). Use the irreducibility of \(M\) in its graph form. Show that you can find either a \(y\) that is \((\rho + \epsilon)\)-good, or a \(y\) that is \(\rho\)-good with \(|S_y| < |S_x|\).
Hint 3 (for (d)). First show a stronger form of (c): every non-negative, nonzero eigenvector of \(M\) is entrywise positive, whatever its eigenvalue. Look at the set of coordinates where such a vector is zero, and use irreducibility.
Hint 4 (for (d)). Let \(u \ge 0\), \(u \ne 0\) with \(Mu = \mu u\). Let \(s\) be the largest number with \(u \ge s\,x\) entrywise, and look at a coordinate where equality holds. Use it to show \(\mu \ge \lambda\), then use (b) to conclude \(\mu = \lambda\).
Hint 5 (for (d)). Now \(u\) and \(x\) are both eigenvectors for \(\lambda\). What does Hint 3 tell you about \(u - s\,x\)?

title: Exercise: ℓ₁ Contraction for Stochastic Matrices
text:
In the Perron–Frobenius exercise, we got a stationary distribution of a random walk from the theory of non-negative matrices. This exercise takes a more probabilistic route. A stochastic matrix never increases \(\ell_1\) distances, and it strictly decreases them when its entries are bounded away from zero. That fact alone is enough.
Setup. A matrix \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is (row-)stochastic if \(P \ge 0\) entrywise and every row sums to \(1\), that is, \(P\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\). The entry \(P_{ij}\) is the probability of moving from state \(i\) to state \(j\). A probability distribution is a vector in \[
\Delta = \{\, p \in \mathbb{R}^n : p \ge 0,\ p^\top \mathbf 1 = 1 \,\}.
\] Distributions are written as row vectors and multiply \(P\) from the left. One step of the Markov chain maps \(p^\top\) to \(p^\top P\). A distribution \(\pi\) is stationary if \(\pi^\top P = \pi^\top\).
For example, the random-walk matrix \(P = D^{-1}A\) of a graph with no isolated vertices is row-stochastic.
Throughout, \(\|v\|_1 = \sum_i |v_i|\).

(a) Weak contraction. Let \(P\) be stochastic. Show that \[
\|v^\top P\|_1 \le \|v\|_1 \qquad \text{for every } v \in \mathbb{C}^n.
\] Deduce two things: - \(p^\top \mapsto p^\top P\) maps \(\Delta\) into \(\Delta\); - every eigenvalue \(\mu\) of \(P\) satisfies \(|\mu| \le 1\).
(b) Existence of a stationary distribution. Let \(P\) be stochastic, and fix any \(p \in \Delta\). For \(T \ge 1\), consider the average \[
\bar p_T^\top = \frac1T \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} p^\top P^t .
\] Show that \(\|\bar p_T^\top P - \bar p_T^\top\|_1 \le 2/T\). Use this to prove that \(P\) has a stationary distribution \(\pi \in \Delta\).
(c) Strict contraction for positive matrices. Let \(Q\) be stochastic with \(Q_{ij} \ge \delta > 0\) for all \(i, j\). Show that \[
\|v^\top Q\|_1 \le (1 - n\delta)\, \|v\|_1 \qquad \text{for every } v \in \mathbb{R}^n \text{ with } v^\top \mathbf 1 = 0.
\]
(d) Uniqueness for irreducible chains. Let \(P\) be stochastic and irreducible: for all \(i, j \in [n]\) there is a positive integer \(k\) such that \((P^k)_{ij} > 0\). Let \[
Q = \Big(\tfrac12 (I + P)\Big)^{n-1}.
\] Show that \(Q\) is stochastic and entrywise positive. Conclude that \(P\) has exactly one stationary distribution \(\pi\), and that \(\pi > 0\) entrywise.
(e) Convergence. Let \(P\) be stochastic, and suppose \(P^m\) is entrywise positive for some \(m \ge 1\). Let \(\delta = \min_{i,j} (P^m)_{ij}\), and let \(\pi\) be the stationary distribution. Show that for every \(p \in \Delta\) and every \(t \ge 0\), \[
\|p^\top P^t - \pi^\top\|_1 \le 2\,(1 - n\delta)^{\lfloor t/m \rfloor}.
\] Explain why this applies to the lazy chain \(\tfrac12(I + P)\) of any irreducible \(P\), but can fail for \(P\) itself.

Hint for (a). Write \((v^\top P)_j = \sum_i v_i P_{ij}\). Apply the triangle inequality, then swap the order of summation. For the eigenvalues, recall that \(P\) and \(P^\top\) have the same eigenvalues.
Hint for (b). Show that \(\bar p_T\) lies in \(\Delta\), and that \(\bar p_T^\top P - \bar p_T^\top\) is a telescoping sum. For the last step, use the compactness of \(\Delta\).
Hint for (c). First explain why \(n\delta \le 1\). Then write \(Q = n\delta\, U + (1 - n\delta)\, R\), where \(U = \frac1n \mathbf 1 \mathbf 1^\top\). Check that \(R\) is stochastic when \(n\delta < 1\), and compute \(v^\top U\) when \(v^\top \mathbf 1 = 0\).
Hint for (d). Expand \((I + P)^{n-1}\) with the binomial theorem. In the directed graph of \(P\), any vertex can reach any other by a path of length at most \(n-1\). For uniqueness, apply (c) to the difference of two stationary distributions.
Hint for (e). The vector \(p - \pi\) sums to zero, and right-multiplying by a stochastic matrix keeps the sum zero. Write \(t = qm + r\) with \(0 \le r < m\). For the last question, consider \(P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\).

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
text:
Conventions (as in the Lecture 2 notes). \(G = (V, E, w)\) is an undirected graph with positive edge weights, \(n = |V|\), no self-loops, and no isolated vertices unless stated otherwise. “Unweighted” means \(w \equiv 1\). We use \[
L = D - A, \qquad L_{rw} = D^{-1}L = I - P, \qquad \mathcal L = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2},
\] with eigenvalues listed in increasing order, \(\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_n\). Recall that \(L_{rw}\) and \(\mathcal L\) have the same spectrum, and that \[
f^\top L f = \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)^2 .
\] Exercises 1–3 are the core. Exercises 4–7 are hand computations and Courant–Fischer practice. Exercises 8–9 practice §3–§6 of the Lecture 2 notes (covered in Lecture 3).

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
section: Exercise 1. The kernel counts connected components
text:
Exercise 1. The kernel counts connected components
Let \(G\) have \(c\) connected components \(V_1, \dots, V_c\).

(a) Prove that \(\ker L = \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1_{V_1}, \dots, \mathbf 1_{V_c}\}\). Conclude that the eigenvalue \(0\) of \(L\) has multiplicity exactly \(c\).
(b) Prove the same for \(L_{rw}\) and \(\mathcal L\). What is \(\ker \mathcal L\)? Be careful about what “multiplicity” means for the non-symmetric matrix \(L_{rw}\).
(c) Conclude that \(\lambda_2 > 0\) if and only if \(G\) is connected, for all three matrices.

Hint. \(Lf = 0\) implies \(f^\top L f = 0\).

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
section: Exercise 2. The top of the spectrum and bipartiteness
text:
Exercise 2. The top of the spectrum and bipartiteness

(a) Prove that \(\lambda_n(\mathcal L) \le 2\), with equality if and only if some connected component of \(G\) is bipartite.
(b) Prove that \(\lambda_n(L) \le 2 d_{\max}\), with equality if and only if some connected component of \(G\) is bipartite and all of its vertices have degree \(d_{\max}\).

Hint 1. Work with \(L_{rw}\) and its Rayleigh quotient in \(L^2(d)\): \(\lambda_n(L_{rw}) = \max_{f \ne 0} \frac{f^\top L f}{f^\top D f}\).
Hint 2. The signless Laplacian \(D + A\) satisfies \(f^\top (D + A) f = \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}(f_i + f_j)^2\). What does \(f^\top(D+A)f = 0\) say about \(f\) on each component?

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
section: Exercise 3. Bipartite spectra are symmetric, and conversely
text:
Exercise 3. Bipartite spectra are symmetric, and conversely

(a) Let \(G\) be bipartite. Prove that the spectrum of \(\mathcal L\) is symmetric about \(1\), with multiplicities: \(\lambda\) and \(2 - \lambda\) are eigenvalues with the same multiplicity. Describe how the eigenvectors correspond.
(b) Prove the converse: if the spectrum of \(\mathcal L\) is symmetric about \(1\), then \(G\) is bipartite. Do not assume \(G\) is connected.
(c) Show by example that the spectrum of the unnormalized \(L\) of a bipartite graph need not be symmetric about any point.

Hint for (a). Let \(S\) be the diagonal matrix with \(S_{ii} = +1\) on one side and \(-1\) on the other. Compute \(SAS\) and \(SDS\).
Hint for (b). Translate the condition into a statement about the eigenvalues of \(P = I - L_{rw}\). Then look at \(\operatorname{tr} P^k\) for odd \(k\), and interpret \((P^k)_{ii}\) in terms of walks.

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
text:
Exercise 4. Spectra by hand
All graphs here are unweighted. For each graph below, compute the full spectrum of \(L\) and of \(\mathcal L\), with multiplicities, and give an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.

(a) The complete graph \(K_n\).
(b) The star \(K_{1,m}\) (\(n = m+1\)).
(c) The complete bipartite graph \(K_{a,b}\).
(d) Find two non-isomorphic graphs with the same \(\mathcal L\)-spectrum. Do they have the same \(L\)-spectrum?

Hint. Look first for eigenvectors supported on a set of vertices with identical neighborhoods and summing to zero there. The trace gives you the last eigenvalue for free.

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
section: Exercise 5. Products, the hypercube, and the grid
text:
Exercise 5. Products, the hypercube, and the grid
The Cartesian product \(G \,\square\, H\) has vertex set \(V_G \times V_H\). Its edges are \((g,h) \sim (g',h)\) with weight \(w_G(g,g')\) whenever \(g \sim g'\), and \((g,h) \sim (g,h')\) with weight \(w_H(h,h')\) whenever \(h \sim h'\).

(a) Prove that \(L_{G \square H} = L_G \otimes I + I \otimes L_H\). Conclude that if \(L_G \varphi = \alpha \varphi\) and \(L_H \psi = \beta \psi\), then \(\varphi \otimes \psi\) is an eigenvector of \(L_{G\square H}\) with eigenvalue \(\alpha + \beta\), and that these give a full eigenbasis.
(b) The hypercube is \(Q_d = K_2 \,\square\, \cdots \,\square\, K_2\) (\(d\) factors), with vertex set \(\{0,1\}^d\). Find all eigenvalues of \(L(Q_d)\) and \(L_{rw}(Q_d)\) with multiplicities. Show that the functions \(\chi_S(x) = (-1)^{\sum_{i \in S} x_i}\), \(S \subseteq [d]\), form an eigenbasis. Check the spectral gap \(2/d\) used in the Lecture 2 notes, §6.5.
(c) Suppose \(G\) is \(d_G\)-regular and \(H\) is \(d_H\)-regular. Express \(L_{rw}(G \square H)\) in terms of \(L_{rw}(G)\) and \(L_{rw}(H)\), and describe its spectrum.
(d) Without regularity, (c) fails. Let \(G = H = P_3\), the path on three vertices, so that \(G \square H\) is the \(3 \times 3\) grid.

Find the spectrum of \(L_{rw}(P_3)\) and an eigenvector \(\varphi\) for the eigenvalue \(1\).
Show that \(\varphi \otimes \mathbf 1\) is not an eigenvector of \(L_{rw}\) of the grid. The formula of (c) with \(d_G = d_H\) would predict eigenvalue \(\tfrac12\).
Compute \(\lambda_2(L_{rw})\) of the \(3\times 3\) grid exactly.


Hint for (d)3. Look for an eigenvector that is odd under the reflection \(x \mapsto -x\) (coordinates \(\{-1,0,1\}\)) and even under \(y \mapsto -y\). It vanishes on the middle column and is determined by two numbers.

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
section: Exercise 6. Trace bounds and test functions
text:
Exercise 6. Trace bounds and test functions

(a) Show that \(\operatorname{tr} L = \sum_i d_i = 2\sum_{e \in E} w_e\) and \(\operatorname{tr} \mathcal L = n\).
(b) Deduce that \(\lambda_2(\mathcal L) \le \frac{n}{n-1} \le \lambda_n(\mathcal L)\).
(c) Show that \(\lambda_2(\mathcal L) = \frac{n}{n-1}\) if and only if \(G\) is a complete graph with all edge weights equal. In particular, among unweighted graphs, equality holds only for \(K_n\).
(d) Using the test function \(f = e_v - \frac1n \mathbf 1\), prove that \[
\lambda_2(L) \le \frac{n}{n-1}\, d_{\min} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lambda_n(L) \ge \frac{n}{n-1}\, d_{\max}.
\] When are these tight?

Hint for (c). If \(\lambda_2 = \frac{n}{n-1}\), part (b) forces all nonzero eigenvalues to be equal. Write \(\mathcal L\) in terms of the unit \(0\)-eigenvector \(u = D^{1/2}\mathbf 1 / \sqrt{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\), then read off \(A\). Use that \(A\) has zero diagonal.

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
text:
Exercise 7. Adding an edge
Let \(H\) be obtained from \(G\) by adding an edge \(e = \{u,v\}\) of weight \(w_e > 0\), or by increasing the weight of an existing edge by \(w_e\).

(a) Prove that \(\lambda_k(L_H) \ge \lambda_k(L_G)\) for every \(k\).
(b) Let \(G\) be unweighted with at least one edge. Using (a) and Exercise 4, prove that \(\lambda_n(L) \ge d_{\max} + 1\). Compare with Exercise 6(d).
(c) Show that (a) fails for \(\mathcal L\): adding one edge to \(P_3\) decreases \(\lambda_3(\mathcal L)\).
(d) Show that adding one edge can also decrease \(\lambda_2(\mathcal L)\). Find an example on four vertices and compute both values exactly. Explain what goes wrong in the proof of (a).

Hint for (a). Write \(L_H - L_G\) as a rank-one matrix and use Courant–Fischer.
Hint for (d). Start from the star \(K_{1,3}\) and join two leaves. Use the symmetry swapping those two leaves to split the eigenvalue problem into small pieces.

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
text:
Exercise 8. The two-state chain, exactly
Let \(0 < a, b \le 1\) and \[
P = \begin{pmatrix} 1-a & a \\ b & 1-b \end{pmatrix}.
\] This is the random walk on a two-vertex weighted graph with self-loops. Like every two-state chain, it is reversible. Consider the continuous-time walk \(H_t = e^{-t(I - P)}\) started at \(\delta_1\), and write \(\mu_t = \delta_1^\top H_t\).

(a) Find the stationary distribution \(\pi\) and the eigenvalues of \(L_{rw} = I - P\). With \(\lambda = a + b\), show that \[
H_t = \mathbf 1 \pi^\top + e^{-\lambda t}\,(I - \mathbf 1\pi^\top).
\]
(b) Let \(s = e^{-\lambda t}\). Compute \(\|\mu_t - \pi\|_{TV}\), \(\chi^2(\mu_t \Vert \pi)\) and \(D(\mu_t \Vert \pi)\) exactly as functions of \(s\), \(\pi_1\), \(\pi_2\).
(c) Check that \(\chi^2\) decays exactly like \(e^{-2\lambda t}\). Why is the theorem of the Lecture 2 notes, §4 an equality here?
(d) Compute the ratio \(2\|\mu_t - \pi\|_{TV} / \sqrt{\chi^2(\mu_t \Vert \pi)}\). When is comparison (1) of the Lecture 2 notes, §3 tight?
(e) Show that \(D(\mu_t\Vert\pi) \sim \frac12 \chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi)\) as \(t \to \infty\). What does this say about comparison (3), \(D \le \log(1+\chi^2) \le \chi^2\), at \(t = 0\) and as \(t \to \infty\)?
(f) Compute \(t_{\rm mix}(\varepsilon)\) exactly, worst case over both starting states. Suppose \(\pi_1 \to 0\). Compare with the two-sided bound of §5.1. Which side is tight? Where does the upper bound lose, given that there are only two states?

Hint for (a). Show that \(E = I - \mathbf 1\pi^\top\) is idempotent and that \(L_{rw} = \lambda E\).

title: Exercises: Computing with Graph Laplacians
text:
Exercise 9. The barbell
The barbell \(B_m\) consists of two disjoint copies of \(K_m\) (\(m \ge 2\)) joined by one bridge edge \(\{u, v\}\), with \(u\) in the first clique and \(v\) in the second. It is unweighted, with \(n = 2m\). Let \(\lambda = \lambda_2(L_{rw})\).

(a) Compute the degrees and \(\mathrm{vol}(V)\). Use a test function to show that \[
\lambda \le \frac{4}{\mathrm{vol}(V)} = \frac{2}{m^2 - m + 1}.
\]
(b) Route canonical paths as follows. Within a clique, use the direct edge. From \(a\) in the first clique to \(b\) in the second, go \(a \to u \to v \to b\), dropping the first or last step if \(a = u\) or \(b = v\); route the reverse pairs the same way. Use unit lengths and the \(\pi\)-weighted canonical-paths bound of the Lecture 2 notes, §6.1, to prove \[
\lambda \ge \frac{\mathrm{vol}(V)}{3m^4} = \frac{2(m^2 - m + 1)}{3m^4}.
\]
(c) Conclude that \(\lambda = \Theta(1/m^2)\) and give upper and lower bounds on \(t_{\rm mix}\) for the continuous-time walk. Compare with \(K_{2m}\) on the same vertex set: how many edges does the barbell lack, and what does that cost in spectral gap?

Hint for (b). There are three kinds of edges: the bridge, clique edges at \(u\) or \(v\), and all other clique edges. Bound the load on each separately, using \(\pi_a \le m/\mathrm{vol}(V)\) for every vertex.

title: Spectral Methods for Machine Learning and Network Analysis
text: Spectral methods study complex systems through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of associated linear operators. Because the theory extends from finite-dimensional linear algebra to infinite-dimensional operators, it gives one framework for problems ranging from graph partitioning and random walks to manifold learning and the numerical solution of differential equations. This graduate course develops that theory and its algorithmic uses, with a focus on spectral graph theory and spectral methods in machine learning.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Last time → today
Lecture 1, §5: heat on a graph, \(\dot u = -Lu\), and on a manifold, \(\partial_t u = -\Delta u\), with \(\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\nabla\). “The Fiedler vector is the last non-uniform heat left.”

Today we make that picture precise:

Graph matrices are \(-\operatorname{div}\nabla\) (for the right measures).
The random walk and the heat kernel; measures vs. functions; the spectral gap.

Next lecture: how fast the walk converges — distances to \(\pi\), mixing time, and bounds on the spectral gap.

~3 min. Conventions as in Lecture 1: P = D^{-1}A row-stochastic, distributions are row vectors on the left, functions are column vectors on the right.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
The gradient

\(G=(V,E,w)\) undirected, connected, weighted graph with \(w_{ij}>0\).
\(\mathbb{R}^V\): the space of real functions on vertices, e.g., potentials such as temperature.
Orient each edge arbitrarily, \(e=(i\to j)\) and define the discrete gradient operator as: \[
\nabla : \mathbb R^V \to \mathbb R^E, \qquad (\nabla f)(e) = f(j) - f(i).
\]

As a matrix: the signed incidence matrix \(B \in \mathbb R^{E\times V}\).


A function on vertices \(\mapsto\) a flow on edges.
\(\ker\nabla\) = constants (connected graph) — “\(\nabla f = 0 \Rightarrow f\) constant.”




Thinking of the graph as a discrete manifold \(M\), this is analogous to the tangent bundle \(TM\) of \(M\). Functions in \(\mathbb{R}^E\) are analogous to vector fields on \(M\). Combinatorially, they can also be interpreted as flows along edges.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
section: Example: \(f\) and \(\nabla f\) on a graph
text:
Example: \(f\) and \(
abla f\) on a graph

Blue = \(f\) at each vertex; orange = \((
abla f)(e) = f(j)-f(i)\) on each oriented edge. Each row of \(B\) is \(-1\) at the tail, \(+1\) at the head: \((Bf)_e = (
abla f)(e)\).

The flow \(
abla f \in \mathbb{R}^E\) can be thought of as a vector field, i.e., a member of the tangent bundle, where \((
abla f)_e\) represents the directional derivative of the function \(f\) along edge \(e\).

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Divergence \(= -\nabla^*\), and the measure matters

In continuous space (e.g., on a smooth compact manifold \(M\) with no boundary), the adjoint of the gradient with respect to the standard \(L^2\) inner product is the negative divergence: \[
\int_M f\,(-\operatorname{div} X) \, dV = \int_M \langle \nabla f, X\rangle \, dV
\]

To make this work on graphs, we need to define appropriate inner products on both the space of functions on vertices and the space of flows on edges.









manifold
graph




on vector fields
metric \(g\)
edge weights: \(\langle X,Y\rangle_w = \sum_e w_e X_eY_e\)


on functions
volume \(dV\)
vertex measure \(m\): \(\langle f,g\rangle_m = \sum_i m_if_ig_i\)




Define \(\nabla^*_m\) by \(\langle\nabla f, X\rangle_w = \langle f,\nabla_m^*X\rangle_m\). Expanding, for coordinate \(i\):
\[
(\nabla_m^* X)_i = \frac{1}{m_i}\Big(\sum_{e \text{ into } i} w_eX_e - \sum_{e \text{ out of } i} w_eX_e\Big) =: -(\operatorname{div}_m X)_i .
\]
Divergence = net weighted outflow per unit vertex mass.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Example: the divergence of \(\nabla f\)

Green = \(\operatorname{div}(\nabla f)_i\) (counting measure, \(m\equiv1\), unweighted): outflow minus inflow at \(i\). E.g. at \(D\): \((-3.5) - \big((-1.5)+(2.5)\big) = -4.5\).

Like in continuous space, \(-\nabla^*\) measures the net outflow of a vector field per unit volume (or vertex mass, in the graph case).


Same graph and same flow X = grad f as two slides ago (orange edge labels unchanged). Now sum signed flow at each vertex: div(X)_i = sum of X_e over edges leaving i, minus sum of X_e over edges entering i. Check: the five div values sum to 0 (telescoping — every edge contributes +X_e to one endpoint and -X_e to the other). Also: div(grad f) = -Lf here, matching div = -nabla^* and L = nabla^* nabla for the counting measure, previewed on the next slide.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Both Laplacians are \(-\operatorname{div}\nabla\)

Proposition. \(\displaystyle(\nabla_m^*\nabla f)_i = \frac1{m_i}\sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)\). Hence

\(m \equiv \mathbf 1\) (counting measure): \(\;\nabla^*\nabla = B^\top WB = D - A = L\), the combinatorial Laplacian;
\(m = d\) (degree measure): \(\;\nabla_d^*\nabla = D^{-1}L = L_{rw}\), the random-walk Laplacian.




Self-adjoint and PSD in \(L^2(m)\) for every \(m\) — nothing to check.
The normalized Laplacian \(\mathcal L = D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\) is \(L_{rw}\) moved to the unweighted space by the isometry \(f\mapsto D^{1/2}f\).




Lecture 1: “a change of which inner product, not a repair of a broken operator.” Now with a reason: the vertex measure is the volume form.


Proof: each edge between i and a neighbor j contributes w_ij (f_i - f_j) regardless of orientation (two cases: e into i or out of i).

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
section: Green’s identity and the Dirichlet form
text:
Green’s identity and the Dirichlet form
By construction (“integration by parts”):
\[
\langle f,\nabla_m^*\nabla g\rangle_m = \langle\nabla f,\nabla g\rangle_w = \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}\,(f_i - f_j)(g_i - g_j)
\]
\[
\longleftrightarrow\qquad \int f\,(-\Delta g) = \int\langle\nabla f,\nabla g\rangle .
\]

No boundary term: graph Laplacians have Neumann boundary conditions built in.


With \(m = \mathbf 1\) (counting measure), we get the energy: \[\langle f,\nabla_m^*\nabla f\rangle_m = \langle\nabla f,\nabla f\rangle_w = \sum w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2 \leftrightarrow \int|\nabla f|^2\]


With \(m = \pi\), \(\pi_i = d_i/\mathrm{vol}(V)\), the normalized degree distribution, we get the Dirichlet form:
\[
\mathcal E(f,g) := \langle f, L_{rw}g\rangle_\pi = \frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)(g_i-g_j).
\]

For later:Weighted-manifold row: \(\Delta_U\) is (minus) the generator of Langevin diffusion with stationary density \(\propto e^{-U}\). \(L_{rw}\) is its discrete twin, with \(\pi\propto d\) playing \(e^{-U}\).

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Sanity check: finite differences

Path, weights \(h^{-2}\): \(\;(Lf)_i = h^{-2}(2f_i - f_{i-1} - f_{i+1})\to -f''\) — the 3-point stencil.
Grid, weights \(h^{-2}\): \(\;(Lf)_{i,j} = h^{-2}(4f_{i,j} - f_{i\pm1,j} - f_{i,j\pm1})\to-\Delta f\) — the 5-point stencil.



Interior grid vertex: degree 4, so L is exactly the 5-point stencil for −Δ. Boundary vertex (green): degree 3; L drops the missing term, equivalent to a ghost value equal to the vertex’s own value, i.e. zero normal derivative (Neumann). Dirichlet would keep the diagonal at 4/h² and lose 1 from the kernel. The cycle’s spectrum (sampled Fourier modes) is computed in Lecture 3, §4.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Recap: properties of the Laplacian
Both \(L\) and \(L_{rw}\) — any \(\nabla_m^*\nabla\) — share three structural facts, for free:

1. Self-adjoint in \(L^2(m)\), for every \(m\): \(L = \nabla_m^*\nabla\) has the form \(A^*A\).



2. Positive semi-definite. \(\langle f,Lf\rangle_m = \langle\nabla f,\nabla f\rangle_w = \sum_{ij}w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2\ge0\).




3. Spectrum is bounded. \(G\) connected \(\Rightarrow\) \(0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\cdots\le\lambda_n\), with \(\ker L = \operatorname{span}(\mathbf 1)\) (\(\lambda_1\) simple). Upper end: \(\lambda_n(L)\le 2d_{\max}\) (Gershgorin); for \(L_{rw}\) and \(\mathcal L\) (\(m=d\)), which are similar to each other: \(\lambda_n\le 2\).




Self-adjoint + PSD + bounded spectrum \(\Rightarrow\) an orthonormal eigenbasis and a well-behaved heat kernel \(H_t = e^{-tL_{rw}}\) — exactly what the rest of this lecture, and the next, leans on.


(1)-(2) are immediate from the A*A form shown on the “Both Laplacians” slide — nothing new to check for any m or any edge weights. (3): kernel = constants because G is connected (gradient slide, §1). Gershgorin for the upper bound: row i of L has diagonal d_i and off-diagonal entries summing to d_i in absolute value, so every eigenvalue lies in some disc [0, 2d_i], hence lambda_n <= 2 d_max. For L_rw = D^{-1}L (similar to the symmetric L = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2}), the same argument with row sums of L_rw equal to 1 gives lambda_n <= 2 directly — this is the bound quoted later (spectral decomposition slide, §2). This slide is pure bookkeeping — the content is all already on screen earlier, just gathered in one place before we start using it.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
The random walk transition matrix

At each step, the random walk picks a neighbor with probability proportional to the edge weight. The probability transition matrix is: \[P = D^{-1}A, \quad P_{ij} = \Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t = i] = w_{ij}/d_i.\]


Stationary distribution is \(\pi_i = d_i/\mathrm{vol}(V)\): \[\pi^\top P = \pi^\top D^{-1}A = \frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\mathbf 1^\top A = \frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\mathbf 1^\top D = \pi^\top.\]

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
One matrix, two actions


Measures (row vectors)
\[\mu^\top\ \mapsto\ \mu^\top P\]
law of \(X_1\) when \(X_0\sim\mu\)

Functions (column vectors)
\[(Pf)(i) = \mathbb E[f(X_1)\mid X_0 = i]\]
local averaging


Canoical pairing \(\langle\mu,f\rangle = \mu^\top f = \mathbb E_\mu f\):
\[
\langle\mu^\top P, f\rangle = \mu^\top Pf = \langle\mu, Pf\rangle .
\]
Evolve the distribution forward and observe, or evolve the observable and average against the start. Same number.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Continuous time: heat kernel
Jump at the rings of a rate-1 Poisson clock:
\[
H_t = \sum_{k\ge0}e^{-t}\frac{t^k}{k!}P^k = e^{-t(I-P)} = e^{-tL_{rw}},\qquad (H_tf)(i) = \mathbb E_i f(X_t).
\]


Backward (functions): \(\partial_tf_t = -L_{rw}f_t\) — Lecture 1’s heat equation.
Forward (measures): \(\mu_t^\top = \mu_0^\top H_t\), \(\;\partial_t\mu_t^\top = -\mu_t^\top L_{rw}\) — master / Fokker–Planck.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Semigroups and generators
We will see that the heat kernel is the special case of a semigroup:
Definition (Semigroup): A family of operators \(\{H_t\}_{t\ge0}\) is a semigroup if:

\(H_0 = I\), and
\(H_{s+t} = H_s H_t\) for all \(s,t\ge0\).

Generator (Markov convention): The generator \(\mathcal{A}\) describes the infinitesimal evolution of the semigroup:
\[\mathcal A = \frac{d}{dt}H_t\big|_{t=0} = P - I = -L_{rw}\]

Sign: we keep the positive operator L_rw ⪰ 0 to match Δ = −div∇ ⪰ 0 from Lecture 1; Markov literature calls A = −L_rw the generator. Semigroup properties used later: H_0 = I, H_{s+t} = H_s H_t, H_t 1 = 1, positivity. Everything below uses only these + self-adjointness, which is why it transfers to diffusions.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Advantages of Continuous Time

Can differentiate by time: \(\partial_t H_t = -L_{rw} H_t\).
Avoids the bipartite problem: eigenvalues of \(H_t\) are in \((0,1]\) rather than \(P\) having \(-1\).

Cycle (\(n\) even), grid, binary tree: all bipartite \(\Rightarrow\) \(P\) has eigenvalue \(-1\).
The discrete walk from a vertex never converges — it alternates sides.

This problem can alternatively be fixed by making the walk lazy:
\[P_{\rm lazy} = \tfrac12(I + P) = I - \tfrac12L_{rw}\],
This has eigenvalues \(1 - \tfrac{\lambda_k}{2}\in[0,1]\).
We work in continuous time; discrete-time statements follow with \(e^{-\lambda}\to 1-\lambda/2\).

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Stationarity and detailed balance
Question: What does self-adjointness in \(L^2(\pi)\) imply for the behavior of the random walk?

Detailed balance:
\[
\pi_iP_{ij} = \frac{w_{ij}}{\mathrm{vol}(V)} = \pi_jP_{ji}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\Pi P = P^\top\Pi,\quad\Pi = \operatorname{diag}(\pi).
\]


\(\Longleftrightarrow\) \(P\), \(L_{rw}\), \(H_t\) are self-adjoint in \(L^2(\pi)\):
\[
\langle f, Pg\rangle_\pi = f^\top\Pi Pg = f^\top P^\top\Pi g = \langle Pf, g\rangle_\pi .
\]
Same fact as \(\nabla_\pi^*\nabla = \mathrm{vol}(V)\,L_{rw}\), now seen probabilistically.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Densities are functions
Write \(\mu = \Pi h\), i.e. \(h = d\mu/d\pi\), \(\;h_i = \mu_i/\pi_i\).

Proposition. If \(\mu_t^\top = \mu_0^\top H_t\) then \(h_t = H_t^*h_0\), with \(H_t^* = \Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi\) the adjoint in \(L^2(\pi)\). For reversible walks \(H_t^* = H_t\): \[h_t = H_th_0 .\] Densities obey the same heat equation as observables.


Proof. \(h_t = \Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi h_0\), and \(\langle f,\Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi g\rangle_\pi = f^\top H_t^\top\Pi g = \langle H_tf,g\rangle_\pi\). Detailed balance: \(\Pi H_t = H_t^\top\Pi\). \(\square\)



\(\mu\mapsto\mu/\pi\) is an isometry from \((\mathbb R^V,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/\pi})\) (measures) to \(L^2(\pi)\) (functions): the Riesz map.
Non-reversible chains: \(h_t\) evolves by the time-reversed semigroup. We’ll meet this again with general Markov semigroups.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
section: Demo: measures vs densities — split and aggregate
text:
Demo: measures vs densities — split and aggregate
open in new tab ↗



One loop: vertex mass –D⁻¹–> value on each edge-end –send–> far end –A–> vertex mass. Measures and densities are the same loop cut at different places. Measures (start at red vertex mass): split (D⁻¹), send, aggregate (A): μᵀ ↦ μᵀD⁻¹A = μᵀP. Mass is conserved. Densities (start at blue value, x = D⁻¹μ = h/vol): send copies, aggregate (A), average (D⁻¹): x ↦ D⁻¹Ax = Px. Constants are preserved. Point out: in density mode the red intermediate Ax_t is exactly μ_{t+1}; the invariant μ_t = D x_t holds at every step. Run it: μ_t → π ∝ degree (uneven red bars), x_t → constant 1/vol (flat blue bars). This makes the previous two slides concrete: π is the fixed point of the measure loop, and densities evolve by the same P as functions (they converge to constants). Graph and starting values are from the old SGT figure (degrees 1,3,2,2; vol = 8). It has a triangle, so the discrete walk is aperiodic and converges.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
section: Spectral decomposition and the Poincaré inequality
text:
Spectral decomposition and the Poincaré inequality
\(L_{rw}\) self-adjoint in \(L^2(\pi)\) \(\Rightarrow\) orthonormal eigenbasis \(\varphi_1 = \mathbf 1,\varphi_2,\dots,\varphi_n\), \(\;0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_n\le2\):
\[
H_tf = \sum_ke^{-\lambda_kt}\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi\varphi_k,\qquad
\mathcal E(f,f) = \sum_k\lambda_k\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2,
\]
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f) = \sum_{k\ge2}\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2 .
\]

Spectral gap \(\lambda := \lambda_2(L_{rw})\). Courant–Fischer:
\[
\lambda = \min_{f\ \text{non-const}}\frac{\mathcal E(f,f)}{\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\ \lambda\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)\le\mathcal E(f,f)\ }
\]
Poincaré inequality: “small gradient \(\Rightarrow\) nearly constant.” Relaxation time \(t_{\rm rel} := 1/\lambda\).



The variance is an energy too. \(\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f) = \sum_{a<b}\pi_a\pi_b(f_a-f_b)^2 = \frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\sum_{a<b}\frac{d_ad_b}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}(f_a-f_b)^2 = \mathcal E_{K_G}(f,f)\), the energy of the complete graph \(K_G\) with weights \(w'_{ab} = d_ad_b/\mathrm{vol}(V)\), which has the same degrees as \(G\) (counting self-loops). So Poincaré is a comparison of two graphs: \(\lambda\,L_{K_G}\preceq L_G\).


Degrees of K_G: Σ_b d_a d_b / vol = d_a (the b = a term is a self-loop, invisible to the energy). K_G has the same stationary distribution π, and its walk is P’ = 1π^T: it jumps straight to stationarity in one step. So λ measures how well G approximates the “ideal mixer” with the same degrees. This K_G is the graph from the old SGT notes (“why Laplacians?”).

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Takeaways

\(L\), \(L_{rw}\): the same \(-\operatorname{div}\nabla\) with different volume measures. Self-adjointness and PSD are automatic.
The walk \(P = D^{-1}A\) acts on measures (row vectors, \(\mu^\top P\)) and on functions (column vectors, \(Pf\)); continuous time gives the heat kernel \(H_t = e^{-tL_{rw}}\) with generator \(-L_{rw}\).
Detailed balance \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(L_{rw}\) self-adjoint in \(L^2(\pi)\) \(\Rightarrow\) densities \(h = \mu/\pi\) evolve like functions: \(h_t = H_th_0\).
Spectral gap \(\lambda = \lambda_2(L_{rw})\) = best Poincaré constant, \(\lambda\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)\le\mathcal E(f,f)\).
Next: measuring convergence to \(\pi\), and what the gap says about mixing times.

title: Laplacians and Random Walks
text:
Operators and the walk
Graph. \(G = (V,E,w)\) undirected, connected; \(d_i = \sum_jw_{ij}\); \(\mathrm{vol}(S) = \sum_{i\in S}d_i\); \(\pi_i = d_i/\mathrm{vol}(V)\), \(\Pi = \operatorname{diag}(\pi)\).
Gradient / divergence. \((\nabla f)(i\to j) = f_j - f_i\); \(\operatorname{div}_m = -\nabla_m^*\) w.r.t. \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_w\) on edges and \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_m\) on vertices. \(\nabla^*\nabla = L = D-A\); \(\nabla_d^*\nabla = L_{rw} = D^{-1}L = I-P\); \(\mathcal L = D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\).
Dirichlet form. \(\mathcal E(f,g) = \langle f,L_{rw}g\rangle_\pi = \frac1{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)(g_i-g_j)\).
Walk. \(P = D^{-1}A\); measures \(\mu^\top P\), functions \(Pf\). Random-walk Laplacian \(L_{rw} = I - P\). Continuous time \(H_t = e^{-tL_{rw}}\), generator \(\mathcal A = P - I = -L_{rw}\). Lazy: \(P_{\rm lazy} = \frac12(I+P)\).
Reversibility. \(\Pi P = P^\top\Pi\); densities \(h = \mu/\pi\) evolve as \(h_t = H_th_0\).
Gap / Poincaré. \(\lambda = \lambda_2(L_{rw}) = \min_f\mathcal E(f,f)/\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)\); \(t_{\rm rel} = 1/\lambda\).

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part I
text:
This note reviews what it means to diagonalize a linear map on a finite-dimensional space, and what can be said when that is impossible.
On a first reading, Sections 1 and 2 are all you need; most of the course uses nothing else. Part II extends Section 2 to infinite dimensions, using the proof strategy of Section 2 almost verbatim, so that proof is worth reading carefully. Sections 3–6 matter whenever matrices are not symmetric: directed graphs, non-reversible Markov chains, and iterative methods.

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part I
text:
1. Notation and conventions

\(\mathbb{F}\) denotes \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\). For \(z \in \mathbb{C}\), \(\bar z\) is the complex conjugate.
\(V\) is a finite-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb{F}\). A linear map \(A : V \to V\) is identified, after choosing a basis, with a matrix in \(\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\). Matrices \(A\) and \(S^{-1}AS\) (\(S\) invertible) are similar: they represent the same map in different bases.
\(\mathbb{F}[t]\) is the ring of polynomials with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}\). A polynomial splits over \(\mathbb{F}\) if it is a product of linear factors \((t - \lambda)\) with \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\).
A scalar \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\) if \(Av = \lambda v\) for some \(v \ne 0\), called an eigenvector. The eigenspace of \(\lambda\) is \(E_\lambda = \ker(A - \lambda I)\), and the set of eigenvalues is the spectrum \(\sigma(A)\). Section 3 develops these notions in general.

The remaining conventions concern inner products, which are needed in Sections 2 and 5.

An inner product on an \(\mathbb{F}\)-vector space \(V\) is a map \(\langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle : V\times V \to \mathbb{F}\) that is linear in the first argument, satisfies \(\langle x, y\rangle = \overline{\langle y, x\rangle}\), and has \(\langle x, x\rangle > 0\) for \(x \neq 0\). (So it is conjugate-linear in the second argument.) The induced norm is \(\|x\| = \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle}\).
On \(\mathbb{F}^n\) the standard inner product is \(\langle x, y\rangle = \sum_i x_i \bar y_i = y^* x\), where \(y^*\) is the conjugate transpose. Over \(\mathbb{R}\), \(y^* = y^\top\).
Two basic identities hold in every inner product space:

Cauchy–Schwarz: \(|\langle x, y\rangle| \le \|x\|\,\|y\|\), with equality iff \(x, y\) are linearly dependent.
Parallelogram law: \(\|x+y\|^2 + \|x-y\|^2 = 2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2\).

\(x \perp y\) means \(\langle x, y\rangle = 0\). For a set \(S\), \(S^\perp = \{x : x \perp s \text{ for all } s \in S\}\). This is always a (closed) subspace.
For a linear map \(A : V \to V\), the adjoint \(A^*\) is the linear map with \(\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, A^* y\rangle\) for all \(x, y\). For matrices with the standard inner product, \(A^*\) is the conjugate transpose. \(A\) is self-adjoint if \(A = A^*\): a real symmetric matrix, or a complex Hermitian matrix.
\(A\) is positive semidefinite (PSD), written \(A \succeq 0\), if it is self-adjoint and \(\langle Ax, x\rangle \ge 0\) for all \(x\). \(A \succeq B\) means \(A - B \succeq 0\).
The Rayleigh quotient of a self-adjoint \(A\) is \(R_A(x) = \dfrac{\langle Ax, x\rangle}{\langle x, x\rangle}\) for \(x \ne 0\).

Example (why self-adjointness shows up everywhere in this course). For an undirected graph \(G = (V, E, w)\), the adjacency matrix \(A\), the Laplacian \(L = D - A\), and the normalized Laplacian \(\mathcal{L} = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}\) are all real symmetric. So are covariance matrices \(\frac1m \sum_i x_i x_i^\top\) and kernel (Gram) matrices \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\). The random-walk matrix \(P = D^{-1}A\) and the random-walk Laplacian \(L_{\mathrm{rw}} = D^{-1}L = I - P\) are not symmetric. They are, however, self-adjoint for the degree-weighted inner product \(\langle x, y\rangle_D = y^* D x\), and this is equivalent to the symmetry of \(\mathcal{L}\) (Section 2.5).

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part I
section: 2. The spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators
text:
2. The spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators
Throughout this section, \(V\) is a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\mathbb{F}\) with \(n = \dim V \ge 1\), and \(A : V \to V\) is linear.
The proof below is variational. It does not use the fundamental theorem of algebra, it produces the Rayleigh-quotient characterization of eigenvalues on which the rest of the course depends, and it is the proof that generalizes to compact operators in Part II. (Section 5 gives a second, algebraic proof via the Schur decomposition; see Corollary 5.3.)

2.1 Two elementary facts
Lemma 2.1. Let \(A\) be self-adjoint.

\(\langle Ax, x\rangle \in \mathbb{R}\) for every \(x\).
Every eigenvalue of \(A\) is real.
Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
If \(W\) is a subspace with \(A W \subseteq W\), then \(A W^\perp \subseteq W^\perp\).

Proof. (1) \(\langle Ax, x\rangle = \langle x, Ax\rangle = \overline{\langle Ax, x\rangle}\). (2) If \(Ax = \lambda x\) with \(x \ne 0\), then \(\lambda \|x\|^2 = \langle Ax, x\rangle \in \mathbb{R}\). (3) If \(Ax = \lambda x\) and \(Ay = \mu y\) with \(\lambda \ne \mu\) (both real by (2)), then \(\lambda\langle x, y\rangle = \langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle = \mu \langle x, y\rangle\), so \(\langle x, y\rangle = 0\). (4) If \(y \in W^\perp\) and \(w \in W\), then \(\langle Ay, w\rangle = \langle y, Aw\rangle = 0\) because \(Aw \in W\). \(\blacksquare\)


2.2 Statement
Theorem 2.2 (Spectral theorem, finite dimensions). Let \(A : V \to V\) be self-adjoint. Then there is an orthonormal basis \(v_1, \dots, v_n\) of \(V\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(A\), with real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n\). Equivalently:

(Matrix form) If \(A \in \mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\) is Hermitian (real symmetric when \(\mathbb{F} = \mathbb{R}\)), then \(A = Q \Lambda Q^*\), where \(Q\) is unitary (real orthogonal when \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\)) with columns \(v_i\) and \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\).
(Spectral decomposition) \(A = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\, v_i v_i^*\). Grouping equal eigenvalues, \(A = \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(A)} \lambda P_\lambda\), where \(P_\lambda\) is the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace \(\ker(A - \lambda I)\). These projections are mutually orthogonal and sum to \(I\).

Note that the real case does not follow from the complex case by a formality: we need the eigenvectors of a real symmetric matrix to be real. The proof below works verbatim over either field.


2.3 Proof
The proof is variational. It never mentions the characteristic polynomial and so does not need the fundamental theorem of algebra. This is the version that generalizes to infinite dimensions.
Lemma 2.3 (Top eigenvector via the Rayleigh quotient). Let \(A\) be self-adjoint on \(V \ne \{0\}\). The function \(x \mapsto \langle Ax, x\rangle\) attains its maximum over the unit sphere \(S = \{x : \|x\| = 1\}\). Any maximizer \(x_\star\) is an eigenvector of \(A\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda_\star = \langle Ax_\star, x_\star\rangle = \max_{x \ne 0} R_A(x)\).
Proof. Choosing an orthonormal basis identifies \(V\) isometrically with \(\mathbb{F}^n\). The unit sphere is therefore closed and bounded, hence compact. The map \(x \mapsto \langle Ax, x\rangle\) is continuous and real-valued (Lemma 2.1), so it attains a maximum \(\lambda_\star\) at some \(x_\star \in S\).
Fix any \(y \perp x_\star\) and a scalar \(s \in \mathbb{F}\). For real \(t\), set \(u(t) = x_\star + t s y\). Then \(\|u(t)\|^2 = 1 + t^2 |s|^2 \|y\|^2\), and by maximality \(\langle A u(t), u(t)\rangle \le \lambda_\star \|u(t)\|^2\). Expanding both sides: \[
\lambda_\star + 2t\,\mathrm{Re}\big(\bar s\,\langle A x_\star, y\rangle\big) + t^2 |s|^2 \langle Ay, y\rangle \;\le\; \lambda_\star + t^2 \lambda_\star |s|^2 \|y\|^2 .
\] Here we used \(\langle Ay, x_\star\rangle = \overline{\langle Ax_\star, y\rangle}\). Cancel \(\lambda_\star\), divide by \(t\), and let \(t \to 0^+\) and \(t \to 0^-\). This gives \(\mathrm{Re}(\bar s \langle Ax_\star, y\rangle) = 0\). Taking \(s = 1\) (and also \(s = i\) in the complex case) yields \(\langle Ax_\star, y\rangle = 0\).
So \(Ax_\star \perp \{x_\star\}^\perp\), which means \(Ax_\star \in \operatorname{span}\{x_\star\}\). Write \(Ax_\star = \mu x_\star\). Then \(\mu = \langle Ax_\star, x_\star\rangle = \lambda_\star\). \(\blacksquare\)
Proof of Theorem 2.2. Induct on \(n = \dim V\). If \(n = 1\), any unit vector works. For \(n > 1\), Lemma 2.3 gives a unit eigenvector \(v_1\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda_1 = \max R_A\). The line \(W = \operatorname{span}\{v_1\}\) is \(A\)-invariant, so by Lemma 2.1(4), \(W^\perp\) is \(A\)-invariant too. The restriction \(A|_{W^\perp}\) is self-adjoint on the \((n-1)\)-dimensional inner product space \(W^\perp\). By induction it has an orthonormal eigenbasis \(v_2, \dots, v_n\) of \(W^\perp\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n\). Each \(\lambda_j\) with \(j \ge 2\) is a value of \(R_A\), so \(\lambda_j \le \lambda_1\). Then \(v_1, \dots, v_n\) is the required basis.
For the matrix form, let \(Q = [v_1 \cdots v_n]\). Then \(Q^*Q = I\) and \(AQ = Q\Lambda\). For the spectral decomposition, expand \(x = \sum_i \langle x, v_i\rangle v_i\) and apply \(A\): \(Ax = \sum_i \lambda_i \langle x, v_i\rangle v_i = \big(\sum_i \lambda_i v_i v_i^*\big) x\). \(\blacksquare\)
Remark 2.4. The same proof shows that \(\lambda_1 = \max_{\|x\|=1} \langle Ax, x\rangle\) and \(\lambda_n = \min_{\|x\|=1} \langle Ax, x\rangle\). Part II (Section 7) replaces the compactness of the unit sphere, which fails in infinite dimensions, with the compactness of the operator.
Remark 2.5 (Beyond self-adjoint). By Theorem 5.2, a complex matrix is unitarily diagonalizable iff it is normal. Non-normal matrices may fail to be diagonalizable at all (Section 6). Even when they are diagonalizable, their eigenvalues can be highly sensitive to perturbation (Section 6.6). Directed graphs and non-reversible Markov chains produce such matrices, and there pseudospectra are often the better tool (Trefethen & Embree).


2.4 Consequences
Throughout, \(A\) is self-adjoint with eigenpairs \((\lambda_i, v_i)\) as in Theorem 2.2, \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n\).
Corollary 2.6 (Functional calculus). For any function \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{F}\), define \(f(A) = \sum_i f(\lambda_i) v_i v_i^*\). This agrees with the obvious definition when \(f\) is a polynomial, so, for example, \(A^k = \sum_i \lambda_i^k v_i v_i^*\). Standard instances:

the heat kernel \(e^{-tL}\);
the pseudoinverse \(L^{+} = \sum_{\lambda_i \ne 0} \lambda_i^{-1} v_i v_i^*\);
the square root \(A^{1/2}\) for \(A \succeq 0\);
spectral projections \(\mathbf{1}_{[a,b]}(A)\).

Corollary 2.7 (Quantities read off the spectrum).

\(\operatorname{tr} A = \sum_i \lambda_i\) and \(\det A = \prod_i \lambda_i\).
\(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}} = \max_i |\lambda_i|\) and \(\|A\|_F^2 = \sum_i \lambda_i^2\).
\(A \succeq 0\) iff all \(\lambda_i \ge 0\) iff \(A = B^*B\) for some \(B\).
\(\operatorname{rank} A\) is the number of nonzero \(\lambda_i\).
\(\ker A\) and \(\operatorname{range} A\) are orthogonal complements, spanned by the eigenvectors with zero and nonzero eigenvalues respectively.

Theorem 2.8 (Courant–Fischer min–max). For \(k = 1, \dots, n\), \[
\lambda_k \;=\; \max_{\substack{S \subseteq V\\ \dim S = k}} \; \min_{x \in S\setminus\{0\}} R_A(x) \;=\; \min_{\substack{T \subseteq V\\ \dim T = n-k+1}} \; \max_{x \in T\setminus\{0\}} R_A(x).
\]
Proof. We prove the max–min formula; the min–max formula follows by applying it to \(-A\).
In eigenvector coordinates, \(x = \sum_i c_i v_i\) and \(R_A(x) = \sum_i \lambda_i |c_i|^2 / \sum_i |c_i|^2\), a weighted average of the eigenvalues.
(\(\ge\)) Take \(S = \operatorname{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_k\}\). Every \(x \in S\) is an average of \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\), so \(R_A(x) \ge \lambda_k\).
(\(\le\)) Let \(S\) be any \(k\)-dimensional subspace and \(U = \operatorname{span}\{v_k, \dots, v_n\}\), which has dimension \(n - k + 1\). Since \(\dim S + \dim U = n+1 > n\), there is a nonzero \(x \in S \cap U\). For this \(x\), \(R_A(x)\) is an average of \(\lambda_k, \dots, \lambda_n\), so \(R_A(x) \le \lambda_k\). Hence \(\min_{S} R_A \le \lambda_k\). \(\blacksquare\)
Example. For a graph Laplacian \(L\) with eigenvalues \(0 = \mu_1 \le \mu_2 \le \dots \le \mu_n\), the min-version gives \(\mu_2 = \min_{x \perp \mathbf{1},\, x \ne 0} \dfrac{\sum_{(u,v)\in E} w_{uv}(x_u - x_v)^2}{\sum_u x_u^2}\). This is the starting point for Cheeger’s inequality and spectral partitioning.
Corollary 2.9 (Weyl’s perturbation inequality). If \(A, B\) are self-adjoint with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1(\cdot) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\cdot)\), then for every \(k\), \[
|\lambda_k(A) - \lambda_k(B)| \le \|A - B\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
Proof. For every \(x \ne 0\), \(R_A(x) = R_B(x) + R_{A-B}(x) \le R_B(x) + \|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\). Take max–min over \(S\) in Theorem 2.8 to get \(\lambda_k(A) \le \lambda_k(B) + \|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\). Swap \(A\) and \(B\) for the other direction. \(\blacksquare\)
Weyl’s inequality controls eigenvalues. Eigenvectors are controlled only relative to the gap separating their eigenvalue from the rest of the spectrum (Davis–Kahan \(\sin\Theta\) theorem; see the separate supplement). We will return to this when analyzing spectral clustering.


2.5 Self-adjointness for a weighted inner product
Theorem 2.2 is stated for an abstract inner product space. Nothing in it refers to the standard inner product on \(\mathbb{F}^n\). This matters because several natural graph matrices are not symmetric, yet are self-adjoint for a different inner product.
Let \(M \in \mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\) be positive definite (\(M = M^*\) and \(M \succ 0\)). Then \(\langle x, y\rangle_M = y^* M x\) is an inner product on \(\mathbb{F}^n\). The adjoint of \(B\) with respect to it is \(M^{-1}B^*M\), because \[
\langle Bx, y\rangle_M = y^* M B x = (M^{-1} B^* M y)^* M x = \langle x, M^{-1}B^*My\rangle_M .
\]
Proposition 2.10. Let \(M \succ 0\) and \(B \in \mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\). The following are equivalent:

\(B\) is self-adjoint with respect to \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_M\);
\(MB\) is self-adjoint (Hermitian) in the usual sense;
\(M^{1/2} B M^{-1/2}\) is self-adjoint in the usual sense.

When they hold, \(B\) has real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n\), and there is a basis of eigenvectors that is orthonormal for \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_M\). Explicitly, if \(u_1, \dots, u_n\) is an orthonormal eigenbasis of \(M^{1/2}BM^{-1/2}\), then \(v_i = M^{-1/2}u_i\) satisfies \(Bv_i = \lambda_i v_i\) and \(v_i^* M v_j = \delta_{ij}\). Courant–Fischer (Theorem 2.8) holds with the Rayleigh quotient \[
R^M_B(x) = \frac{\langle Bx, x\rangle_M}{\langle x, x\rangle_M} = \frac{x^* MB\, x}{x^* M x}.
\]
Proof.

(1)⇔(2): (1) says \(M^{-1}B^*M = B\), i.e., \(B^*M = MB\). Since \((MB)^* = B^*M\), this is exactly (2).
(2)⇔(3): \(M^{1/2}BM^{-1/2} = M^{-1/2}(MB)M^{-1/2}\). A congruence by the invertible Hermitian matrix \(M^{-1/2}\) preserves being Hermitian, and so does its inverse.
The spectral statements: apply Theorem 2.2 to \(C = M^{1/2}BM^{-1/2}\). From \(Cu_i = \lambda_i u_i\) we get \(B(M^{-1/2}u_i) = \lambda_i M^{-1/2}u_i\), and \(v_i^*Mv_j = u_i^* u_j = \delta_{ij}\). Alternatively, apply Theorem 2.2 directly to the inner product space \((\mathbb{F}^n, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_M)\). \(\blacksquare\)

Conceptually, \(U = M^{1/2}\) is an isometry from \((\mathbb{F}^n, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_M)\) onto \((\mathbb{F}^n, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\), since \(\langle Ux, Uy\rangle = y^*Mx = \langle x, y\rangle_M\). The operator \(B\) in the first picture corresponds to \(UBU^{-1} = M^{1/2}BM^{-1/2}\) in the second. Isometries preserve adjoints, so \(B\) is self-adjoint in one picture iff it is in the other. Proposition 2.10 is this observation written in coordinates.
Application: the random-walk and normalized Laplacians. Let \(G\) be a weighted graph with no isolated vertices, so \(D \succ 0\). Define the degree inner product \(\langle x, y\rangle_D = \sum_u d_u\, x_u \bar y_u\), and the random-walk Laplacian \[
L_{\mathrm{rw}} = D^{-1}L = I - D^{-1}A.
\] In the analysis-on-graphs convention, this is simply “the Laplacian”: \((L_{\mathrm{rw}} f)(u) = f(u) - \frac{1}{d_u}\sum_v w_{uv} f(v)\). Apply Proposition 2.10 with \(M = D\) and \(B = L_{\mathrm{rw}}\):

\(D L_{\mathrm{rw}} = L\), which is symmetric, so condition (2) holds. So \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}\) is self-adjoint for \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_D\).
\(D^{1/2} L_{\mathrm{rw}} D^{-1/2} = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2} = \mathcal{L}\). So condition (3) is precisely the symmetry of the normalized Laplacian in the standard inner product.

Thus the statements “\(L_{\mathrm{rw}}\) is self-adjoint on \((\mathbb{R}^V, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_D)\)” and “\(\mathcal{L}\) is symmetric on \((\mathbb{R}^V, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\)” are the same fact, seen through the isometry \(x \mapsto D^{1/2}x\). Consequences:

\(L_{\mathrm{rw}}\) and \(\mathcal{L}\) have the same (real) eigenvalues.
The eigenvectors are related by \(v = D^{-1/2}u\), and the eigenvectors of \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}\) are \(D\)-orthogonal.
Equivalently, the \(v_i\) solve the generalized eigenproblem \(Lv = \lambda Dv\).
The Rayleigh quotient becomes \[
R^D_{L_{\mathrm{rw}}}(x) = \frac{x^\top L x}{x^\top D x} = \frac{\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E} w_{uv}(x_u - x_v)^2}{\sum_u d_u x_u^2}.
\] This is the form that appears in Cheeger’s inequality. The constant vector \(\mathbf 1\) spans the bottom eigenspace for a connected graph, and “orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1\)” now means \(\langle x, \mathbf 1\rangle_D = \sum_u d_u x_u = 0\).
The same holds for \(P = D^{-1}A = I - L_{\mathrm{rw}}\). Since the stationary distribution of the random walk is \(\pi_u = d_u / \sum_v d_v\), \(P\) is self-adjoint on \(\ell^2(\pi)\). More generally, a Markov chain is reversible iff its transition matrix is self-adjoint on \(\ell^2(\pi)\).

Which picture to use is a matter of convenience. \(\mathcal{L}\) is convenient for computation and for applying matrix inequalities stated for symmetric matrices. \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}\) with \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_D\) is convenient for interpretation, because its eigenvectors are functions on the vertices, not reweighted ones. This is also the version that generalizes to infinite graphs and to manifolds, via \(\ell^2(V, d)\) and \(L^2(\mu)\).
