text:
3. Eigenvalues and the characteristic polynomial
Section 2 treated self-adjoint maps, where everything works out as well as possible. We now drop symmetry and ask what survives. Throughout Sections 3–6, \(V\) is a vector space over \(\mathbb{F}\) of dimension \(n \ge 1\) and \(A : V \to V\) is linear. No inner product is needed until Section 5. Choosing a basis identifies \(A\) with a matrix in \(\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\). Changing the basis replaces the matrix by a similar one, \(S^{-1}AS\) with \(S\) invertible. Every notion below is invariant under similarity, so it belongs to the linear map, not the matrix.

3.1 Eigenvalues and multiplicities
A scalar \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\) if \(Av = \lambda v\) for some \(v \ne 0\), called an eigenvector. The eigenspace is \(E_\lambda = \ker(A - \lambda I)\). Its dimension \(g_\lambda = \dim E_\lambda\) is the geometric multiplicity of \(\lambda\). The set of eigenvalues is the spectrum \(\sigma(A)\).
The characteristic polynomial is \[
p_A(t) = \det(tI - A) = t^n - (\operatorname{tr} A)\, t^{n-1} + \dots + (-1)^n \det A .
\] It is monic of degree \(n\). It is similarity invariant, since \(\det(tI - S^{-1}AS) = \det\big(S^{-1}(tI - A)S\big) = \det(tI - A)\). And \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue iff \(A - \lambda I\) is singular iff \(p_A(\lambda) = 0\). The multiplicity \(a_\lambda\) of \(\lambda\) as a root of \(p_A\) is its algebraic multiplicity. If \(p_A\) splits over \(\mathbb{F}\), i.e., factors into linear factors \(p_A(t) = \prod_{\lambda \in \sigma(A)} (t - \lambda)^{a_\lambda}\), then comparing coefficients gives \[
\operatorname{tr} A = \sum_\lambda a_\lambda \lambda, \qquad \det A = \prod_\lambda \lambda^{a_\lambda}.
\]
Existence of eigenvalues depends on the field.

Over \(\mathbb{C}\), the fundamental theorem of algebra says \(p_A\) always splits. So every linear map on a nonzero complex vector space has an eigenvalue.
Over \(\mathbb{R}\), this fails. The rotation \(R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\) has \(p(t) = t^2 - 2\cos\theta\, t + 1\), with no real roots unless \(\theta \in \pi\mathbb{Z}\). The standard remedy is to regard a real matrix as a complex one. Its eigenvalues are then real or come in conjugate pairs.

Lemma 3.1. Eigenvectors \(v_1, \dots, v_k\) belonging to distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) are linearly independent.
Proof. Suppose not, and take a nontrivial relation \(\sum_{i\in I} c_i v_i = 0\) with the fewest nonzero terms. It has at least two terms. Pick \(j \in I\) and apply \(A - \lambda_j I\): this gives \(\sum_{i \in I} c_i(\lambda_i - \lambda_j)v_i = 0\). The new relation is nontrivial, since \(\lambda_i \ne \lambda_j\) for \(i \ne j\), and has fewer terms. That contradicts minimality. \(\blacksquare\)
Lemma 3.2. For every eigenvalue \(\lambda\), \(1 \le g_\lambda \le a_\lambda\).
Proof. Extend a basis of \(E_\lambda\) to a basis of \(V\). In this basis, \(A = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda I_{g} & * \\ 0 & C\end{pmatrix}\) with \(g = g_\lambda\). So \(p_A(t) = (t - \lambda)^{g}\, p_C(t)\), and \((t-\lambda)^g\) divides \(p_A\). \(\blacksquare\)


3.2 Diagonalizability
\(A\) is diagonalizable (over \(\mathbb{F}\)) if \(V\) has a basis of eigenvectors of \(A\). Equivalently, \(A = S\Lambda S^{-1}\) with \(\Lambda\) diagonal. The columns of \(S\) are the eigenvectors.
Theorem 3.3. \(A\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{F}\) iff \(p_A\) splits over \(\mathbb{F}\) and \(g_\lambda = a_\lambda\) for every \(\lambda \in \sigma(A)\). In particular, if \(A\) has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues in \(\mathbb{F}\), it is diagonalizable.
Proof. (⇒) If \(A = S\Lambda S^{-1}\), then \(p_A(t) = \prod_i (t - \Lambda_{ii})\) splits, and \(g_\lambda = \#\{i : \Lambda_{ii} = \lambda\} = a_\lambda\).
(⇐) By Lemma 3.1, the sum \(\sum_\lambda E_\lambda\) is direct. Its dimension is \(\sum_\lambda g_\lambda = \sum_\lambda a_\lambda = \deg p_A = n\). So it is all of \(V\), and the union of bases of the \(E_\lambda\) is an eigenbasis. \(\blacksquare\)
Examples from graphs. Let \(\vec P_n\) be the directed path \(1 \to 2 \to \dots \to n\) and \(\vec C_n\) the directed cycle.

The adjacency matrix of \(\vec P_n\) is nilpotent. Its only eigenvalue is \(0\), with \(a_0 = n\) but \(g_0 = 1\), so it is not diagonalizable over any field.
The adjacency matrix of \(\vec C_n\) is a permutation matrix with \(p(t) = t^n - 1\). It has \(n\) distinct complex eigenvalues (the \(n\)-th roots of unity), so it is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{C}\). For \(n \ge 3\) it is not diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{R}\).
Undirected graphs give symmetric matrices, which are always diagonalizable, in an orthonormal basis (Section 2).

Why diagonalizability matters. If \(A = S\Lambda S^{-1}\), then \[
A^k = S\Lambda^k S^{-1}, \qquad e^{tA} = S e^{t\Lambda}S^{-1},
\] so linear dynamics \(x_{k+1} = Ax_k\) or \(\dot x = Ax\) decouple into \(n\) scalar ones. The catch for non-symmetric \(A\) is that \(S\) need not be orthogonal. An ill-conditioned \(S\) (large \(\kappa(S) = \|S\|\,\|S^{-1}\|\)) makes these formulas numerically and quantitatively misleading. See Section 6.6.

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part I
section: 4. Polynomials in \(A\) and the minimal polynomial
text:
4. Polynomials in \(A\) and the minimal polynomial

4.1 The minimal polynomial
For \(q(t) = \sum_k c_k t^k \in \mathbb{F}[t]\), set \(q(A) = \sum_k c_k A^k\). The map \(q \mapsto q(A)\) respects sums and products. So all polynomials in \(A\) commute with each other and with \(A\). Two further facts:

If \(Av = \lambda v\), then \(q(A)v = q(\lambda)v\).
\(q(S^{-1}AS) = S^{-1}q(A)S\).

Some nonzero polynomial annihilates \(A\): the \(n^2 + 1\) matrices \(I, A, \dots, A^{n^2}\) live in the \(n^2\)-dimensional space \(\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\), so they are linearly dependent.
Proposition 4.1. There is a unique monic polynomial \(m_A\) of least degree with \(m_A(A) = 0\), the minimal polynomial of \(A\). A polynomial \(q\) satisfies \(q(A) = 0\) iff \(m_A\) divides \(q\).
Proof. Let \(m\) be a monic annihilating polynomial of least degree. For any \(q\) with \(q(A) = 0\), divide: \(q = sm + r\) with \(\deg r < \deg m\). Then \(r(A) = q(A) - s(A)m(A) = 0\), so \(r = 0\) by minimality. Uniqueness: two such \(m\) divide each other and are monic. \(\blacksquare\)
Proposition 4.2. The roots of \(m_A\) in \(\mathbb{F}\) are exactly the eigenvalues of \(A\) in \(\mathbb{F}\).
Proof. If \(Av = \lambda v\) with \(v \ne 0\), then \(0 = m_A(A)v = m_A(\lambda)v\), so \(m_A(\lambda) = 0\).
Conversely, if \(m_A(\lambda) = 0\), write \(m_A(t) = (t - \lambda)q(t)\). Since \(\deg q < \deg m_A\), \(q(A) \ne 0\). Pick \(w\) with \(v = q(A)w \ne 0\). Then \((A - \lambda I)v = m_A(A)w = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)


4.2 The primary decomposition
The engine behind everything that follows is a statement about coprime polynomials.
Lemma 4.3 (Kernel splitting). Suppose \(q(A) = 0\) and \(q = q_1q_2\) with \(\gcd(q_1, q_2) = 1\). Then \[
V = \ker q_1(A) \oplus \ker q_2(A).
\] Both summands are \(A\)-invariant. The projection onto \(\ker q_1(A)\) along \(\ker q_2(A)\) is a polynomial in \(A\).
Proof. By Bézout, there are polynomials \(a, b\) with \(aq_1 + bq_2 = 1\), so \(I = a(A)q_1(A) + b(A)q_2(A)\). For any \(v\), \[
v = \underbrace{b(A)q_2(A)v}_{=:v_1} + \underbrace{a(A)q_1(A)v}_{=:v_2}.
\] Here \(q_1(A)v_1 = b(A)q(A)v = 0\), so \(v_1 \in \ker q_1(A)\). Similarly, \(v_2 \in \ker q_2(A)\).
If \(v\) lies in both kernels, both terms vanish, so \(v = 0\). The sum is therefore direct, and the projection onto the first summand is \(b(A)q_2(A)\). Invariance: if \(q_i(A)v = 0\), then \(q_i(A)Av = Aq_i(A)v = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)
Corollary 4.4 (Primary decomposition). If \(q(A) = 0\) and \(q = q_1 \cdots q_r\) with the \(q_i\) pairwise coprime, then \[
V = \ker q_1(A) \oplus \dots \oplus \ker q_r(A).
\] Each summand is \(A\)-invariant, and the projections \(P_i\) onto the summands are polynomials in \(A\). In particular, they commute with \(A\), with each other, and with anything that commutes with \(A\).
Proof. Induct on \(r\), applying Lemma 4.3 to \(q_1\) and \(q_2\cdots q_r\) (which are coprime). \(\blacksquare\)


4.3 Diagonalizability via the minimal polynomial
Theorem 4.5. The following are equivalent:

\(A\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{F}\).
\(m_A\) splits over \(\mathbb{F}\) with distinct roots: \(m_A(t) = \prod_{\lambda \in \sigma(A)}(t - \lambda)\).
\(A\) is annihilated by some polynomial that splits over \(\mathbb{F}\) with distinct roots.

Proof.

(1)⇒(2): Let \(q(t) = \prod_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)} (t-\lambda)\). Then \(q(A)\) kills every eigenvector, hence every vector of an eigenbasis. So \(q(A) = 0\) and \(m_A\) divides \(q\). By Proposition 4.2, every factor of \(q\) appears in \(m_A\), so \(m_A = q\).
(2)⇒(3) is trivial.
(3)⇒(1): If \(q(A) = 0\) with \(q = \prod_{i}(t - \mu_i)\) and the \(\mu_i\) distinct, the factors are pairwise coprime. Corollary 4.4 gives \(V = \bigoplus_i \ker(A - \mu_i I)\), a direct sum of eigenspaces. \(\blacksquare\)

Corollary 4.6.

If \(A\) is diagonalizable and \(W\) is an \(A\)-invariant subspace, then \(A|_W\) is diagonalizable. (Proof: \(m_A(A|_W) = 0\), so criterion (3) applies.)
Projections (\(A^2 = A\)) and involutions (\(A^2 = I\)) are diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{R}\). Matrices with \(A^k = I\) are diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{C}\), since \(t^k - 1\) has \(k\) distinct complex roots. This covers every permutation matrix, and in particular \(\vec C_n\).

Proposition 4.7 (Simultaneous diagonalization). If \(A\) and \(B\) are diagonalizable and \(AB = BA\), then they have a common eigenbasis.
Proof. \(B\) preserves each eigenspace \(E_\lambda\) of \(A\): if \(Av = \lambda v\), then \(A(Bv) = BAv = \lambda Bv\). By Corollary 4.6(1), \(B|_{E_\lambda}\) is diagonalizable. Choose an eigenbasis of \(B|_{E_\lambda}\) inside each \(E_\lambda\). Its vectors are eigenvectors of \(A\) too, and together they form a basis of \(V = \bigoplus_\lambda E_\lambda\). \(\blacksquare\)


4.4 The Cayley–Hamilton theorem
Theorem 4.8 (Cayley–Hamilton). \(p_A(A) = 0\). Consequently, \(m_A\) divides \(p_A\), and \(\deg m_A \le n\).
Proof. Let \(\operatorname{adj}\) denote the adjugate (transposed cofactor matrix), so that \(\operatorname{adj}(M)\,M = \det(M)\,I\). Apply this to \(M = tI - A\): \[
\operatorname{adj}(tI - A)\,(tI - A) = p_A(t)\, I .
\] The entries of \(\operatorname{adj}(tI - A)\) are polynomials of degree \(\le n-1\) in \(t\). Write \(\operatorname{adj}(tI - A) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_k t^k\) with constant matrices \(B_k\), and \(p_A(t) = \sum_{k=0}^n c_k t^k\). Set \(B_{-1} = B_n = 0\) and compare coefficients of \(t^k\): \[
B_{k-1} - B_kA = c_k I, \qquad k = 0, \dots, n.
\] Multiply the \(k\)-th identity on the right by \(A^k\) and sum over \(k\). The left side telescopes: \[
p_A(A) = \sum_{k=0}^n \big(B_{k-1}A^k - B_kA^{k+1}\big) = B_{-1} - B_nA^{n+1} = 0. \qquad\blacksquare
\]
The proof uses only polynomial identities, so it holds over any field. The tempting one-liner “substitute \(t = A\) into \(\det(tI - A)\)” is not a proof, since \(\det(A\cdot I - A)\) would be a scalar, whereas \(p_A(A)\) is a matrix.
Corollary 4.9. If \(p_A(t) = \prod_\lambda (t - \lambda)^{a_\lambda}\), then \[
m_A(t) = \prod_\lambda (t-\lambda)^{k_\lambda}, \qquad 1 \le k_\lambda \le a_\lambda.
\] The exponents \(k_\lambda\) are identified in Section 6 as the size of the largest Jordan block for \(\lambda\).
Examples. For \(A = \operatorname{diag}(1,1,2)\): \(p_A = (t-1)^2(t-2)\) and \(m_A = (t-1)(t-2)\). For the \(n\times n\) Jordan block with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) (Section 6): \(p_A = m_A = (t-\lambda)^n\).
Application: distinct eigenvalues bound the diameter. Let \(G\) be a connected graph with nonnegative edge weights, adjacency matrix \(A\), and diameter \(\mathrm{diam}(G)\). Then \[
\mathrm{diam}(G) \le (\text{number of distinct eigenvalues of } A) - 1.
\]
Proof.

Since \(A\) is symmetric, it is diagonalizable (Section 2). By Theorem 4.5, \(\deg m_A\) equals the number of distinct eigenvalues.
Let \(D = \mathrm{diam}(G)\). Fix \(u\) and vertices \(w_0 = u, w_1, \dots, w_D\) along a shortest path, so \(d(u, w_k) = k\).
The entry \((A^j)_{u w_k}\) sums the weights of walks of length \(j\) from \(u\) to \(w_k\). So it is \(0\) for \(j < k\) and positive for \(j = k\).
If \(\sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j A^j = 0\), look at entry \((u, w_D)\): only \(j = D\) contributes, so \(c_D = 0\). Then look at \((u, w_{D-1})\) to get \(c_{D-1} = 0\), and so on.
So \(I, A, \dots, A^D\) are linearly independent, and \(\deg m_A \ge D + 1\). \(\blacksquare\)

The same fact underlies Krylov methods. Conjugate gradient and Lanczos applied to a symmetric matrix terminate, in exact arithmetic, after at most (number of distinct eigenvalues) steps.

section: 5. Triangularization: the Schur decomposition and normal matrices

5. Triangularization: the Schur decomposition and normal matrices
Not every matrix is diagonalizable, but over \(\mathbb{C}\) every matrix is triangularizable, even by a unitary change of basis. In this section \(V\) carries an inner product (Section 1).
Theorem 5.1 (Schur). Let \(A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\). There is a unitary \(U\) and an upper triangular \(T\) with \[
A = UTU^*.
\] The diagonal entries of \(T\) are the eigenvalues of \(A\), repeated according to algebraic multiplicity, and they can be placed in any prescribed order. If \(A\) is real and \(p_A\) splits over \(\mathbb{R}\), then \(U\) can be taken real orthogonal and \(T\) real.
Proof. Induct on \(n\); the case \(n = 1\) is trivial. Let \(\lambda\) be the eigenvalue to be placed first. (One exists by the fundamental theorem of algebra, or by the splitting hypothesis in the real case.) Let \(v\) be a unit eigenvector, and complete it to a unitary matrix \([v\ W]\). Since \(W^*Av = \lambda W^*v = 0\), \[
[v\ W]^* A\, [v\ W] = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda & v^*AW \\ 0 & W^*AW \end{pmatrix}.
\] Now \(p_{W^*AW}(t) = p_A(t)/(t - \lambda)\). So by induction, \(W^*AW = U_1T_1U_1^*\), with the remaining eigenvalues in the prescribed order. Then \(U = [v\ \ WU_1]\) works. The diagonal of \(T\) lists the eigenvalues with multiplicity because \(p_A = p_T = \prod_i (t - T_{ii})\). \(\blacksquare\)
Unlike the Jordan form below, the Schur form is computed stably in practice: it is what the QR algorithm produces.
Theorem 5.2 (Normal matrices). \(A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) is unitarily diagonalizable (\(A = U\Lambda U^*\) with \(U\) unitary and \(\Lambda\) diagonal) iff \(A\) is normal: \(AA^* = A^*A\).
Proof. (⇒) Diagonal matrices commute with their adjoints, so \(AA^* = U\Lambda\bar\Lambda U^* = A^*A\).
(⇐) Write \(A = UTU^*\) by Schur. Then \(T\) is normal and upper triangular. Compare the \((1,1)\) entries of \(T^*T\) and \(TT^*\): \[
|t_{11}|^2 = (T^*T)_{11} = (TT^*)_{11} = \sum_{j} |t_{1j}|^2 .
\] So \(t_{1j} = 0\) for \(j > 1\). The lower-right \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) block is again normal and upper triangular, so induction shows \(T\) is diagonal. \(\blacksquare\)
Corollary 5.3. A Hermitian matrix is unitarily diagonalizable with real eigenvalues. (Here \(T = T^*\) is upper triangular, so it is diagonal with real entries.) A real symmetric matrix therefore has real eigenvalues, so \(p_A\) splits over \(\mathbb{R}\), and the real case of Theorem 5.1 gives a real orthogonal eigenbasis.
This is a second proof of the spectral theorem (Theorem 2.2), at least over \(\mathbb{C}\) and for real symmetric matrices. The variational proof of Section 2 is the more useful one: it avoids the fundamental theorem of algebra, produces the Courant–Fischer characterization along the way, and extends to infinite dimensions (Part II).
Examples of normal matrices.

Hermitian and skew-Hermitian matrices.
Unitary matrices, including permutation matrices. The adjacency matrix of \(\vec C_n\) is unitarily diagonalized by the discrete Fourier basis \(\big(\omega^{jk}/\sqrt n\big)_{j}\) with \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}\).
Circulant matrices, i.e., polynomials in the cyclic shift. These are the adjacency matrices of Cayley graphs of \(\mathbb{Z}_n\), and they are all diagonalized by the same Fourier basis.

The adjacency matrix of a directed graph is normal only in special cases. The directed path is not even diagonalizable.

6. The Jordan canonical form
When \(A\) is not diagonalizable, the best one can do by similarity is block diagonal form with Jordan blocks. Throughout this section, assume \(p_A\) splits over \(\mathbb{F}\), which is automatic over \(\mathbb{C}\). Write \(p_A(t) = \prod_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}(t-\lambda)^{a_\lambda}\).

6.1 Generalized eigenspaces
The generalized eigenspace of \(\lambda \in \sigma(A)\) is \[
G_\lambda = \ker (A - \lambda I)^{a_\lambda} \;\supseteq\; E_\lambda .
\]
Theorem 6.1 (Generalized eigenspace decomposition).

\(V = \bigoplus_{\lambda \in \sigma(A)} G_\lambda\), and each \(G_\lambda\) is \(A\)-invariant.
\(\lambda\) is the only eigenvalue of \(A|_{G_\lambda}\), and \(\dim G_\lambda = a_\lambda\).
The projections \(P_\lambda\) onto \(G_\lambda\) along \(\bigoplus_{\mu\ne\lambda} G_\mu\) are polynomials in \(A\), and \(\sum_\lambda P_\lambda = I\).

Proof. (1) and (3): By Cayley–Hamilton, \(p_A(A) = 0\). The factors \((t - \lambda)^{a_\lambda}\) are pairwise coprime, so Corollary 4.4 applies.
(2): If \(v \in G_\lambda\) and \(Av = \mu v\) with \(v \ne 0\), then \(0 = (A-\lambda I)^{a_\lambda}v = (\mu - \lambda)^{a_\lambda}v\), so \(\mu = \lambda\). Hence \(p_{A|_{G_\lambda}}(t) = (t - \lambda)^{\dim G_\lambda}\). In a basis adapted to the decomposition in (1), \(A\) is block diagonal, so \(p_A = \prod_\lambda p_{A|_{G_\lambda}}\). Comparing exponents gives \(\dim G_\lambda = a_\lambda\). \(\blacksquare\)


6.2 The Jordan–Chevalley decomposition
Theorem 6.2 (Jordan–Chevalley). There are unique linear maps \(S\) and \(N\) with:

\(A = S + N\);
\(S\) diagonalizable and \(N\) nilpotent (\(N^k = 0\) for some \(k\));
\(SN = NS\).

Moreover, \(S\) and \(N\) are polynomials in \(A\).
Proof. Existence. With \(P_\lambda\) as in Theorem 6.1, set \(S = \sum_\lambda \lambda P_\lambda\) and \(N = A - S\). Both are polynomials in \(A\), so they commute. \(S\) acts as \(\lambda I\) on \(G_\lambda\), so it is diagonalizable. On \(G_\lambda\), \(N\) acts as \(A - \lambda I\), and \((A - \lambda I)^{a_\lambda} = 0\) there. So \(N^{\max_\lambda a_\lambda} = 0\).
Uniqueness. Suppose \(A = S' + N'\) is another such decomposition.

\(S'\) and \(N'\) commute with \(S' + N' = A\), hence with every polynomial in \(A\), in particular with \(S\) and \(N\).
So \(S - S' = N' - N\). The left side is a difference of commuting diagonalizable maps, hence diagonalizable by Proposition 4.7. The right side is a difference of commuting nilpotent maps, hence nilpotent: expand \((N' - N)^{2k}\) with the binomial theorem.
A map that is both diagonalizable and nilpotent is \(0\). \(\blacksquare\)

\(S = \sum_\lambda \lambda P_\lambda\) is the non-normal analogue of the spectral decomposition in Theorem 2.2. The differences are that the \(P_\lambda\) are oblique projections, not orthogonal ones, and that there is a nilpotent correction \(N\). When \(A\) is normal, \(N = 0\) and the \(P_\lambda\) are orthogonal.


6.3 Nilpotent maps
For \(\lambda \in \mathbb{F}\) and \(s \ge 1\), the Jordan block \(J_s(\lambda) \in \mathbb{F}^{s\times s}\) has \(\lambda\) on the diagonal, \(1\) on the superdiagonal, and \(0\) elsewhere: \[
J_s(\lambda) = \lambda I_s + N_s, \qquad N_s e_1 = 0,\quad N_s e_j = e_{j-1}\ (j \ge 2).
\] \(N_s\) is nilpotent, with \(N_s^{s-1} \ne 0 = N_s^s\). So \(\dim\ker N_s^k = \min(k, s)\).
Theorem 6.3 (Structure of nilpotent maps). Let \(N : V \to V\) be nilpotent. There are vectors \(u_1, \dots, u_r \in V\) and integers \(m_1, \dots, m_r \ge 0\) such that:

the vectors \(N^{m_i}u_i, \dots, Nu_i, u_i\), for \(i = 1, \dots, r\), form a basis of \(V\);
\(N^{m_i + 1}u_i = 0\) for each \(i\).

In this basis, listed chain by chain, \(N = \bigoplus_i J_{m_i+1}(0)\).
Proof. Induct on \(\dim V\). If \(N = 0\), any basis works with all \(m_i = 0\). Otherwise, \(N\) is not injective (it is nilpotent), so \(\operatorname{range} N \subsetneq V\). \(N\) maps \(\operatorname{range} N\) into itself nilpotently.
Step 1: apply induction to \(\operatorname{range} N\). We get \(v_1, \dots, v_s \in \operatorname{range} N\) and integers \(\ell_i \ge 0\) such that the vectors \(N^j v_i\) (\(0 \le j \le \ell_i\)) form a basis of \(\operatorname{range} N\), and \(N^{\ell_i+1}v_i = 0\). Write \(v_i = Nu_i\).
Step 2: the lifted chains are independent. Let \(L\) be the list of vectors \(N^j u_i\) for \(0 \le j \le \ell_i + 1\). Suppose \(\sum_{i,j} c_{ij} N^j u_i = 0\). Apply \(N\): \[
\sum_{i,j} c_{ij}N^{j+1}u_i = \sum_i \sum_{j=0}^{\ell_i} c_{ij} N^j v_i = 0,
\] where the terms with \(j = \ell_i + 1\) vanish because \(N^{\ell_i+1}v_i = 0\). The remaining vectors are the basis of \(\operatorname{range} N\), so \(c_{ij} = 0\) for \(j \le \ell_i\). What is left is \(\sum_i c_{i,\ell_i+1} N^{\ell_i+1}u_i = \sum_i c_{i,\ell_i+1}N^{\ell_i}v_i = 0\). These vectors are also part of that basis, so the remaining coefficients vanish too.
Step 3: complete with kernel vectors. Extend \(L\) to a basis of \(V\) by vectors \(w_1, \dots, w_p\). Each \(Nw_k\) lies in \(\operatorname{range} N\), which is spanned by \(N(L)\). So \(Nw_k = Nx_k\) for some \(x_k \in \operatorname{span} L\). Put \(u_{s+k} = w_k - x_k\). Then \(Nu_{s+k} = 0\), and \(L, u_{s+1}, \dots, u_{s+p}\) still spans \(V\) and has \(\dim V\) elements, so it is a basis.
The theorem holds with \(m_i = \ell_i + 1\) for \(i \le s\) and \(m_{s+k} = 0\). For the matrix form, in the chain \(N^{m}u, \dots, Nu, u\), \(N\) sends each vector to the previous one and the first to \(0\). That is exactly \(N_{m+1}\). \(\blacksquare\)


6.4 The Jordan canonical form
Theorem 6.4 (Jordan canonical form). If \(p_A\) splits over \(\mathbb{F}\), there is a basis of \(V\) in which \[
A = \bigoplus_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}\ \bigoplus_{i=1}^{g_\lambda} J_{s_{\lambda,i}}(\lambda).
\] The block sizes are determined by \(A\): for each \(\lambda\) and \(k \ge 1\), \[
\#\{i : s_{\lambda,i} \ge k\} = \dim\ker(A - \lambda I)^k - \dim\ker(A-\lambda I)^{k-1}.
\] Hence the Jordan form is unique up to the order of the blocks. Two matrices are similar iff they have the same Jordan form.
Proof. Existence. By Theorem 6.1, it suffices to work on each \(G_\lambda\). There, \(N = (A - \lambda I)|_{G_\lambda}\) is nilpotent. Theorem 6.3 gives a basis of \(G_\lambda\) in which \(N = \bigoplus_i J_{s_i}(0)\), so \(A|_{G_\lambda} = \lambda I + N = \bigoplus_i J_{s_i}(\lambda)\).
The counting formula. \((A - \lambda I)^k\) is invertible on \(G_\mu\) for \(\mu \ne \lambda\). So only the \(\lambda\)-blocks contribute to its kernel, and \(\dim\ker J_s(\lambda - \lambda)^k = \dim \ker N_s^k = \min(k,s)\). Hence \[
\dim\ker(A-\lambda I)^k = \sum_i \min(k, s_{\lambda,i}).
\] Taking differences in \(k\) counts the blocks of size \(\ge k\).
The number of blocks for \(\lambda\) is the \(k=1\) count, \(\dim E_\lambda = g_\lambda\).
Similarity. The dimensions of \(\ker(A - \lambda I)^k\) are similarity invariants, so similar matrices have the same Jordan form. The converse is clear. \(\blacksquare\)
Corollary 6.5 (Reading the invariants off the Jordan form). For each \(\lambda \in \sigma(A)\):

\(a_\lambda\) is the total size of the \(\lambda\)-blocks;
\(g_\lambda\) is the number of \(\lambda\)-blocks;
the exponent \(k_\lambda\) of \((t-\lambda)\) in \(m_A\) is the size of the largest \(\lambda\)-block.

(The last follows because \(m_A\) of a block diagonal matrix is the least common multiple of the blocks’ minimal polynomials, and \(m_{J_s(\lambda)} = (t-\lambda)^s\).) In particular, \(A\) is diagonalizable iff every Jordan block is \(1\times1\), iff \(k_\lambda = 1\) for all \(\lambda\), iff \(g_\lambda = a_\lambda\) for all \(\lambda\). This recovers Theorems 3.3 and 4.5.
Example. \(\vec P_n\) is a single block \(J_n(0)\) (Exercise 5). A matrix with \(p_A = (t-2)^4\), \(\dim\ker(A - 2I) = 2\) and \(\dim\ker(A-2I)^2 = 4\) has Jordan form \(J_2(2)\oplus J_2(2)\).


6.5 Powers and exponentials
Since \(\lambda I\) and \(N_s\) commute and \(N_s^s = 0\), the binomial theorem gives \[
J_s(\lambda)^k = \sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}N_s^j, \qquad e^{tJ_s(\lambda)} = e^{t\lambda}\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\frac{t^j}{j!}N_s^j .
\] So the entries of \(A^k\) are combinations of \(k^j\lambda^k\) with \(j <\) (block size). Consequences:

\(A^k \to 0\) iff the spectral radius \(\rho(A) = \max_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|\lambda|\) is less than \(1\). (A block \(J_s(\lambda)\) with \(|\lambda| < 1\) still decays, because \(k^{s-1}|\lambda|^k \to 0\).)
More precisely, if \(\rho(A) > 0\), then \(\|A^k\| \asymp k^{s-1}\rho(A)^k\) as \(k\to\infty\), where \(s\) is the largest block among the eigenvalues of modulus \(\rho(A)\). The limit \(\|A^k\|^{1/k} \to \rho(A)\) is Gelfand’s formula.
For a Markov chain \(P\), convergence to stationarity is governed by the eigenvalues with \(|\lambda| < 1\). For a non-reversible chain, Jordan blocks contribute polynomial prefactors, and \(\kappa(S)\) can produce long transients before the asymptotic rate kicks in. Reversible chains avoid both problems because \(P\) is self-adjoint in \(\ell^2(\pi)\) (Section 2.5).



6.6 A warning: the Jordan form is unstable
The Jordan form is a discontinuous function of the matrix. Let \(A_\varepsilon = J_n(0) + \varepsilon\, e_ne_1^\top\). Then \(p_{A_\varepsilon}(t) = t^n - \varepsilon\). So \(A_\varepsilon\) has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues \(\varepsilon^{1/n}e^{2\pi ij/n}\) and is diagonalizable. For \(n = 10\) and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-10}\), a perturbation of size \(10^{-10}\) moves the eigenvalues by \(0.1\).
Compare the Hermitian case, where Weyl’s inequality (Corollary 2.9) says eigenvalues move by at most \(\|E\|\). For diagonalizable matrices, the general statement interpolates between the two:
Theorem 6.6 (Bauer–Fike). If \(A = S\Lambda S^{-1}\) is diagonalizable, then every eigenvalue \(\mu\) of \(A + E\) satisfies \[
\min_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|\mu - \lambda| \le \kappa(S)\,\|E\|, \qquad \kappa(S) = \|S\|\,\|S^{-1}\|.
\]
Proof. Assume \(\mu \notin \sigma(A)\) and let \((A + E)v = \mu v\) with \(v \ne 0\). Then \[
v = -(A - \mu I)^{-1}Ev = -S(\Lambda - \mu I)^{-1}S^{-1}Ev.
\] Taking norms, \(1 \le \kappa(S)\,\|E\| \,/\min_\lambda|\lambda - \mu|\). \(\blacksquare\)
For normal matrices \(S\) is unitary, so \(\kappa(S) = 1\). In practice, one therefore works with the Schur form, singular values, or pseudospectra (Trefethen & Embree) rather than the Jordan form. The Jordan form remains the right theoretical description of what \(A\) does.

7. Exercises

Show that a real matrix that is diagonalizable by a real orthogonal matrix must be symmetric. Conclude that Theorem 2.2 characterizes real symmetric matrices.
Prove the min–max half of Theorem 2.8 directly, without passing to \(-A\).
Let \(A \succeq 0\). Show that \(A\) has a unique PSD square root. (Hint: any PSD square root commutes with \(A\), so it preserves each eigenspace of \(A\).)
Using Section 2.5, prove that the random-walk matrix \(P = D^{-1}A\) of a connected graph has eigenvalues in \([-1,1]\), that \(1\) is a simple eigenvalue, and that \(-1\) is an eigenvalue iff the graph is bipartite.
Compute the characteristic polynomial, minimal polynomial, and Jordan form of the adjacency matrices of the directed path \(\vec P_n\) and the directed cycle \(\vec C_n\). Find an eigenbasis of \(\vec C_n\) over \(\mathbb{C}\).
Assume \(p_A\) splits. Show that \(A\) is diagonalizable iff \(\ker(A - \lambda I)^2 = \ker(A - \lambda I)\) for every \(\lambda \in \sigma(A)\).
Show that every square matrix is similar to its transpose. (Hint: \(J_s(\lambda)^\top\) is similar to \(J_s(\lambda)\) via the reversal permutation.)
Show that commuting matrices \(A, B \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) have a common eigenvector, and deduce that they can be simultaneously upper-triangularized by a unitary matrix.
Show that \(A^k \to 0\) iff \(\rho(A) < 1\), and give an example where \(\rho(A) < 1\) but \(\|A^k\|\) first grows to \(10^6\) before decaying. (Hint: \(2\times 2\) upper triangular.)
Show that the number of distinct eigenvalues of the Laplacian of a connected graph is also at least \(\mathrm{diam}(G) + 1\). Compute both sides for the path \(P_n\) and the complete graph \(K_n\).

title: Random Walks and Their Convergence
text:
This lecture turns Lecture 1’s qualitative picture (“the Fiedler vector is the last non-uniform heat left”) into theorems. We (1) derive the graph matrices as discrete \(-\operatorname{div}\nabla\), (2) set up the random walk as a semigroup with generator \(D^{-1}L\) and make precise the duality between measures and functions, (3) define the distances we use to measure convergence and the mixing time, (4) prove that the spectral gap controls \(\chi^2\) decay, (5) derive what this says about \(\ell_1\) and entropy, and (6) compute upper and lower bounds on the gap for the cycle, grid and binary tree via test functions and canonical paths, then compare against the true mixing times.
Conventions (as in Lecture 1). \(P = D^{-1}A\) is row-stochastic; probability distributions are row vectors acting from the left (\(\mu^\top P\)); functions are column vectors acted on from the right (\(Pf\)). Sign convention: we work with the positive operator \(L_{rw} = D^{-1}L \succeq 0\), matching \(\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\nabla \succeq 0\) from Lecture 1. The Markov-process literature calls \(\mathcal A = -L_{rw} = P - I\) “the generator”; we flag the sign wherever it matters.
Running notation.

title: Random Walks and Their Convergence
text:
1. Graph matrices as differential operators
Lecture 1 §5 put two heat equations side by side: \(\dot u = -Lu\) on a graph and \(\partial_t u = -\Delta u\) on a manifold, with \(\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}\). Today we make that analogy literal: each graph matrix is \(-\operatorname{div}\circ\operatorname{grad}\) for an appropriate choice of measures.

1.1 Gradient
Orient each edge arbitrarily, \(e = (i\to j)\). The gradient \(\nabla:\mathbb R^V\to\mathbb R^E\) is \[
(\nabla f)(e) = f(j) - f(i), \qquad e = (i\to j).
\] As a matrix this is the signed edge–vertex incidence matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{E\times V}\), \(B_{e,j}=+1\), \(B_{e,i}=-1\). It is the discrete analog of \(\nabla f\): a function on vertices produces a “vector field” on edges. Its kernel (on a connected graph) is exactly the constants — the discrete version of “\(\nabla f = 0 \Rightarrow f\) constant on a connected domain.”


1.2 Divergence is minus the adjoint — and the adjoint depends on the measures
In the continuum, \(\operatorname{div}\) is defined as \(-\nabla^*\), the adjoint taken in \(L^2\) of the volume measure (that is the integration-by-parts identity \(\int \langle \nabla f, X\rangle\,dV = -\int f\,\operatorname{div}X\,dV\)). On a graph we must choose two measures:

an edge measure — the weights \(w_e\) (play the role of the metric / conductivity): \(\langle X,Y\rangle_w = \sum_e w_e X_e Y_e\);
a vertex measure \(m\) (plays the role of the volume form): \(\langle f,g\rangle_m = \sum_i m_i f_i g_i\).

The adjoint \(\nabla^*_m: \mathbb R^E\to\mathbb R^V\) is defined by \(\langle \nabla f, X\rangle_w = \langle f, \nabla_m^* X\rangle_m\). Expanding the left side, \[
\sum_{e=(i\to j)} w_e\,(f_j-f_i)\,X_e = \sum_i f_i\Big(\sum_{e \text{ into } i} w_eX_e - \sum_{e\text{ out of } i} w_eX_e\Big),
\] so \((\nabla_m^*X)_i = \frac{1}{m_i}\big(\text{net } w\text{-weighted flow into } i\big)\), and \(\operatorname{div}_m := -\nabla_m^*\) is “net weighted outflow per unit vertex mass.”


1.3 The Laplacians
Proposition. \(\nabla_m^*\nabla\) is the operator \((\nabla_m^*\nabla f)_i = \frac{1}{m_i}\sum_{j\sim i} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)\). In particular:

\(m \equiv 1\) (counting measure): \(\nabla^*\nabla = B^\top W B = D - A = L\);
\(m = d\) (degree measure), equivalently \(m=\pi\) (constant rescaling is harmless): \(\nabla^*_d\nabla = D^{-1}L = L_{rw}\), the random-walk Laplacian (so named because \(L_{rw} = I - P\)).

Proof. Plug \(X=\nabla f\) into the formula above: an edge \(e=(k\to i)\) contributes \(w_e(f_i-f_k)\) and an edge \(e=(i\to j)\) contributes \(-w_e(f_j-f_i) = w_e(f_i-f_j)\); either way each neighbor \(j\) contributes \(w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)\), independent of the orientation. \(\square\)
So \(L\) and \(L_{rw}\) are the same differential operator \(-\operatorname{div}\nabla\) with respect to two different volume measures, and \(\mathcal L = D^{1/2}L_{rw}D^{-1/2}\) is \(L_{rw}\) transported to the unweighted space by the isometry \(f\mapsto D^{1/2}f\) from \(L^2(d)\) to \(L^2(\mathbf 1)\). This is the “change of inner product, not a repair” remark from Lecture 1, now with a reason.
Green’s identity / Dirichlet form. By construction, \[
\langle f, \nabla_m^*\nabla g\rangle_m = \langle \nabla f,\nabla g\rangle_w = \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)(g_i-g_j),
\] the analog of \(\int f\,(-\Delta g) = \int\langle\nabla f,\nabla g\rangle\). Note there is no boundary term: graph Laplacians come with natural (Neumann) boundary conditions built in. The quadratic form \(\|\nabla f\|_w^2\) is the energy \(\int|\nabla f|^2\); with \(m=\pi\) (normalized) it is our Dirichlet form \(\mathcal E(f,f)\).
Self-adjointness for free. \(\nabla_m^*\nabla\) is self-adjoint and PSD in \(L^2(m)\) for every \(m\) — there is nothing to check. Which \(m\) you pick decides which matrix you write down.

The weighted-manifold row is the one that matters later: \(\Delta_U = \Delta + \langle\nabla U,\nabla\cdot\rangle\) is (minus) the generator of Langevin diffusion with stationary density \(\propto e^{-U}\). \(L_{rw}\) is its discrete analog, with \(\pi\propto d\) playing the role of \(e^{-U}\).


1.5 Sanity check: finite differences
Path on \(h\mathbb Z\) with weights \(w = h^{-2}\): \((Lf)_i = h^{-2}(2f_i - f_{i-1}-f_{i+1}) \to -f''\). The \(k\times k\) grid with weights \(h^{-2}\) gives the 5-point stencil for \(-\Delta\) on the square, with Neumann boundary conditions. And the cycle \(C_n\) is the discretized circle: eigenvectors \(\cos(2\pi jx/n)\), \(\sin(2\pi jx/n)\), eigenvalues \(2-2\cos(2\pi j/n)\approx(2\pi j/n)^2\) — exactly the Fourier modes of \(-d^2/d\theta^2\) (Lecture 1’s heat demo overlaid these).

2. The generator and the measure/function duality

2.1 Two objects, two actions
The discrete-time walk has \(\Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t=i] = P_{ij} = w_{ij}/d_i\). \(P\) acts on two different kinds of objects:

measures (distributions), row vectors: \(\mu^\top \mapsto \mu^\top P\), i.e., \(\Pr[X_1=\cdot]\) when \(X_0\sim\mu\);
functions (observables), column vectors: \(f\mapsto Pf\), \((Pf)(i) = \sum_j P_{ij}f(j) = \mathbb E[f(X_1)\mid X_0=i]\) — a local averaging operator.

They are linked by the pairing \(\langle\mu,f\rangle = \mu^\top f = \mathbb E_\mu f\): \[
\langle \mu^\top P, f\rangle = \mu^\top P f = \langle \mu, Pf\rangle .
\] Evolving the measure forward and observing, or evolving the observable “backward” and averaging against the initial measure, give the same number. In operator language: the action on measures is the transpose (pairing-adjoint) of the action on functions.


2.2 Continuous time, the generator, the semigroup
Let the walk jump at the times of a rate-1 Poisson clock, each jump according to \(P\). Then \[
H_t := \sum_{k\ge0} e^{-t}\frac{t^k}{k!}P^k = e^{-t(I-P)} = e^{-tL_{rw}},
\] \[
(H_tf)(i) = \mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_0=i],\qquad \mu_t^\top = \mu_0^\top H_t .
\] Differentiating:

backward (Kolmogorov) equation on functions: \(\partial_t f_t = -L_{rw}f_t\) — the heat equation of Lecture 1, now with \(L_{rw}\);
forward (master / Fokker–Planck) equation on measures: \(\partial_t \mu_t^\top = -\mu_t^\top L_{rw}\).

The generator in the Markov-process convention is \(\mathcal A = \lim_{t\to0}(H_t - I)/t = P - I = -L_{rw}\), with \[
(\mathcal A f)(i) = \sum_j P_{ij}\big(f(j)-f(i)\big) = \frac{1}{d_i}\sum_{j\sim i} w_{ij}(f_j-f_i),
\] “average of neighbors minus self” — the discrete \(+\Delta\) (analyst’s sign, negative semidefinite). \((H_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a Markov semigroup: \(H_0=I\), \(H_{s+t}=H_sH_t\), \(H_t\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\), \(f\ge0\Rightarrow H_tf\ge0\). These four properties are all we’ll use; that’s why the arguments below transfer verbatim to diffusions later in the course.
Why continuous time (or laziness). The cycle with \(n\) even, the grid and the binary tree are all bipartite, so \(P\) has eigenvalue \(-1\) and the discrete-time walk started at a vertex never converges (it alternates sides). Two standard fixes, equivalent for our purposes: the continuous-time walk above, or the lazy walk \(P_{\rm lazy} = \frac12(I+P) = I - \frac12 L_{rw}\), whose eigenvalues \(1-\lambda_k/2\) lie in \([0,1]\).


2.3 Stationarity and reversibility
\(\pi_i = d_i/\mathrm{vol}(V)\) is stationary: \((\pi^\top P)_j = \sum_i \frac{d_i}{\mathrm{vol}}\frac{w_{ij}}{d_i} = \frac{d_j}{\mathrm{vol}}\). Moreover detailed balance holds: \[
\pi_iP_{ij} = \frac{w_{ij}}{\mathrm{vol}(V)} = \pi_jP_{ji}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \Pi P = P^\top\Pi .
\] Equivalently \(P\) (and hence \(L_{rw}\), \(H_t\)) is self-adjoint in \(L^2(\pi)\): \(\langle f,Pg\rangle_\pi = f^\top\Pi Pg = f^\top P^\top\Pi g = \langle Pf,g\rangle_\pi\). This is the same fact as §1.3 (\(L_{rw} = \nabla_\pi^*\nabla\)), seen probabilistically.


2.4 Densities are functions — and they evolve like functions
Write a measure via its density with respect to \(\pi\): \(h = d\mu/d\pi\), i.e., \(\mu = \Pi h\), \(h_i = \mu_i/\pi_i\).
Proposition (duality). If \(\mu_t^\top = \mu_0^\top H_t\), then \(h_t = H_t^* h_0\), where \(H_t^* = \Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi\) is the adjoint of \(H_t\) in \(L^2(\pi)\). For a reversible walk \(H_t^*=H_t\), so \[
\boxed{\ h_t = H_t h_0\ }
\] — densities obey the same (backward) heat equation as observables.
Proof. \(\mu_t = H_t^\top\mu_0 = H_t^\top\Pi h_0\), so \(h_t = \Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi h_0\). For any \(f,g\): \(\langle f,\Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi g\rangle_\pi = f^\top H_t^\top \Pi g = \langle H_t f, g\rangle_\pi\), so this is the \(L^2(\pi)\)-adjoint. Reversibility gives \(\Pi H_t = H_t^\top\Pi\). \(\square\)
Geometric picture. Measures live naturally in \(\mathbb R^V\) with the inner product \(\langle\mu,\nu\rangle_{1/\pi} = \sum_i \mu_i\nu_i/\pi_i\); functions in \(L^2(\pi)\). The map \(\mu\mapsto \mu/\pi\) is an isometry between them (the Riesz map), and it intertwines the forward and backward evolutions. (Up to the normalization by \(\mathrm{vol}(V)\), these are the degree-weighted inner products \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_D\) and \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{D^{-1}}\).) From now on we analyze convergence entirely in terms of \(h_t = H_th_0\) in \(L^2(\pi)\).
Forward pointer (Markov semigroups). Without reversibility, \(h_t\) evolves under \(H_t^*\), the semigroup of the time-reversed chain, which is a different Markov semigroup with the same \(\pi\). Everything in §4–5 goes through using \(\mathcal E(f,f) = \langle f, L_{rw}f\rangle_\pi\) (which only sees the symmetric part of the generator); we’ll redo this for general Markov semigroups and for diffusions.


2.5 Spectral decomposition, the gap, Poincaré
\(L_{rw}\) is self-adjoint in \(L^2(\pi)\), so it has an \(L^2(\pi)\)-orthonormal eigenbasis \(\varphi_1=\mathbf 1,\varphi_2,\dots,\varphi_n\) with \(0=\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_n\), and \[
H_t f = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_kt}\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi\,\varphi_k,\qquad \mathcal E(f,f) = \sum_k \lambda_k\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2,
\] \[
\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f) = \|f-\mathbb E_\pi f\|_\pi^2 = \sum_{k\ge2}\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2 .
\] (Facts, from the review notes / exercises: \(\lambda_2>0\) iff \(G\) connected; \(\lambda_n\le 2\) with equality iff a connected component is bipartite.)
Spectral gap and Poincaré inequality. By Courant–Fischer, \[
\lambda = \lambda_2(L_{rw}) = \min_{f\ \text{non-const}}\frac{\mathcal E(f,f)}{\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)} = \min_{f\ \text{non-const}}\frac{\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2}{\min_c \sum_i d_i(f_i-c)^2},
\] i.e., \(\lambda\) is the best constant in the Poincaré inequality \(\lambda\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)\le\mathcal E(f,f)\) — “a function with small gradient is nearly constant.” The relaxation time is \(t_{\rm rel} := 1/\lambda\).
The variance is an energy too. Expanding the variance over pairs, \[
\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f) = \frac12\sum_{a,b}\pi_a\pi_b(f_a-f_b)^2 = \frac1{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\sum_{\{a,b\}}\frac{d_ad_b}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}(f_a-f_b)^2 = \mathcal E_{K_G}(f,f),
\] the Dirichlet form (same \(1/\mathrm{vol}(V)\) normalization) of the complete graph \(K_G\) with weights \(w'_{ab} = d_ad_b/\mathrm{vol}(V)\). Each vertex has degree \(\sum_bd_ad_b/\mathrm{vol}(V) = d_a\) in \(K_G\) (the \(b=a\) term is a self-loop, invisible to the energy), so \(K_G\) has the same degrees, hence the same \(\pi\), as \(G\) — and its walk \(P' = \mathbf 1\pi^\top\) reaches stationarity in a single step. The Poincaré inequality is therefore a comparison between two graphs with the same degrees, \[
\lambda\,L_{K_G}\preceq L_G ,
\] and \(\lambda\) measures how well \(G\) approximates this “ideal mixer.”

3. Measuring convergence; mixing time
For a distribution \(\mu\) with density \(h=\mu/\pi\):








Distance
Measure form
Density form




total variation
\(\lVert\mu-\pi\rVert_{TV} = \tfrac12\lVert\mu-\pi\rVert_1 = \max_{S\subseteq V}\lvert\mu(S)-\pi(S)\rvert\)
\(\tfrac12\,\mathbb E_\pi\lvert h-1\rvert\)


chi-squared
\(\chi^2(\mu\Vert\pi) = \sum_i \frac{(\mu_i-\pi_i)^2}{\pi_i} = \lVert\mu-\pi\rVert_{1/\pi}^2\)
\(\operatorname{Var}_\pi(h) = \lVert h-1\rVert^2_\pi\)


relative entropy (KL)
\(D(\mu\Vert\pi) = \sum_i\mu_i\log\frac{\mu_i}{\pi_i}\)
\(\operatorname{Ent}_\pi(h) = \mathbb E_\pi[h\log h] - \mathbb E_\pi h\log\mathbb E_\pi h\)



Each is \(\mathbb E_\pi\Phi(h)\) for a convex \(\Phi\) with \(\Phi(1)=0\) (an \(f\)-divergence): \(\Phi(x) = \frac12|x-1|,\ (x-1)^2,\ x\log x\).
Starting from a point mass \(\mu=\delta_x\) (\(h = \mathbf 1_x/\pi_x\)): \[
\|\delta_x-\pi\|_{TV} = 1-\pi_x\le1,\qquad D(\delta_x\Vert\pi) = \log\frac{1}{\pi_x},\qquad \chi^2(\delta_x\Vert\pi) = \frac1{\pi_x}-1 .
\] On a bounded-degree graph \(\pi_x\approx 1/n\): the three initial distances are \(O(1)\), \(\log n\), and \(n\). Keep this in mind — it is the whole story of §5.
Lemma (comparisons). For all \(\mu\): 1. \(2\|\mu-\pi\|_{TV}\le\sqrt{\chi^2(\mu\Vert\pi)}\); 2. (Pinsker) \(\|\mu-\pi\|_{TV}\le\sqrt{\tfrac12 D(\mu\Vert\pi)}\); 3. \(D(\mu\Vert\pi)\le\log\big(1+\chi^2(\mu\Vert\pi)\big)\le\chi^2(\mu\Vert\pi)\).
Proof. (1) Cauchy–Schwarz in \(L^2(\pi)\): \(\mathbb E_\pi|h-1|\le(\mathbb E_\pi(h-1)^2)^{1/2}\). (3) Jensen for the concave \(\log\) under \(\mu\): \(D = \mathbb E_\mu\log h\le\log\mathbb E_\mu h = \log\mathbb E_\pi h^2 = \log(1+\operatorname{Var}_\pi h)\). (2) is Pinsker’s inequality (standard; proof in any information-theory text — reduce to two points by data processing, then calculus). \(\square\)
Lemma (monotonicity). For convex \(\Phi\), \(t\mapsto\mathbb E_\pi\Phi(H_th)\) is non-increasing. Proof. \(H_t\) is an averaging operator, so Jensen gives \(\Phi(H_th)\le H_t\Phi(h)\) pointwise; and \(\mathbb E_\pi H_tg = \mathbb E_\pi g\) by stationarity. Use the semigroup property for general \(s<t\). \(\square\) (For TV this is the \(\ell_1\)-contraction from Lecture 1’s exercise.) Monotone, yes — but for rates we need more than convexity: we need a differential inequality, and that is where \(\chi^2\) and entropy are special (§4–5). TV is the distance we want; \(\chi^2\) and entropy are the ones we can differentiate.
Mixing time. Worst case over starting points: \[
d(t) := \max_{x\in V}\|\delta_xH_t-\pi\|_{TV},\qquad t_{\rm mix}(\varepsilon) := \min\{t: d(t)\le\varepsilon\},
\] \[
t_{\rm mix}:=t_{\rm mix}(1/4).
\] Analogously \(t_2(\varepsilon)\) and \(t_{\rm ent}(\varepsilon)\) with \(\sqrt{\chi^2}\) or \(D\) in place of TV. (Worst case over \(x\) = worst case over all \(\mu\), by convexity.) Same definitions for the lazy discrete chain with \(P_{\rm lazy}^t\). Remark for later: \(d(t)\) is essentially submultiplicative, so \(t_{\rm mix}(\varepsilon)\le\lceil\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rceil\,t_{\rm mix}\) (Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Ch. 4); the choice \(1/4\) is a convention.

title: Random Walks and Their Convergence
text:
4. The spectral gap controls \(\chi^2\)
Theorem. For every \(h\) and \(t\ge0\): \(\operatorname{Var}_\pi(H_th)\le e^{-2\lambda t}\operatorname{Var}_\pi(h)\). Equivalently \(\chi^2(\mu_t\Vert\pi)\le e^{-2\lambda t}\chi^2(\mu_0\Vert\pi)\). The rate is sharp: equality holds for \(h = 1+\epsilon\varphi_2\).
Proof 1 (spectral). \(\operatorname{Var}_\pi(H_th) = \sum_{k\ge2}e^{-2\lambda_kt}\langle h,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2\le e^{-2\lambda t}\sum_{k\ge2}\langle h,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2\). \(\square\)
Proof 2 (Dirichlet form — the template for the rest of the course). Let \(h_t = H_th\); \(\mathbb E_\pi h_t\) is constant. Then \[
\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}_\pi(h_t) = 2\langle h_t-\mathbb E_\pi h_t,\ \partial_th_t\rangle_\pi = -2\langle h_t-c, L_{rw}h_t\rangle_\pi = -2\,\mathcal E(h_t,h_t),
\] using \(L_{rw}\mathbf 1 = 0\) and self-adjointness. Poincaré gives \(\mathcal E(h_t,h_t)\ge\lambda\operatorname{Var}_\pi(h_t)\), so \(\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}\le-2\lambda\operatorname{Var}\); Grönwall. \(\square\)
Proof 2 never diagonalizes anything: it uses only (i) “variance dissipates at rate \(2\mathcal E\)” and (ii) the functional inequality \(\mathcal E\ge\lambda\operatorname{Var}\). Replace the pair (Var, Poincaré) by (Ent, log-Sobolev) and you get §5.3; replace the graph by a manifold and you get the Bakry–Émery program. In fact the theorem is an equivalence: if \(\operatorname{Var}(H_th)\le e^{-2ct}\operatorname{Var}(h)\) for all \(h\), differentiating at \(t=0\) gives \(\mathcal E\ge c\operatorname{Var}\), so \(c\le\lambda\).

4.1 The heat flow is the gradient flow of the energy in the \(\chi^2\) geometry
Equip densities with the Hilbert structure of \(L^2(\pi)\), so that the squared distance to equilibrium is \(\|h-1\|_\pi^2 = \chi^2(\mu\Vert\pi)\), and let \(F(h) = \frac12\mathcal E(h,h)\) be the Dirichlet energy. Since \(F(h+\epsilon v) = F(h)+\epsilon\langle L_{rw}h,v\rangle_\pi+O(\epsilon^2)\), the \(L^2(\pi)\)-gradient is \(\nabla_\pi F(h) = L_{rw}h\), and the gradient flow \(\partial_th = -\nabla_\pi F(h)\) is exactly the heat equation for densities, \(h_t = H_th_0\). (Equivalently, the implicit-Euler / minimizing-movement scheme \(h_{k+1} = \arg\min_h\{F(h)+\frac1{2\tau}\|h-h_k\|_\pi^2\} = (I+\tau L_{rw})^{-1}h_k\) converges to \(H_t\).)
In this language the Poincaré inequality says \(F(h)\ge\frac\lambda2\|h-\mathbb E_\pi h\|_\pi^2\): the energy is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex transverse to its minimizers. The theorem of §4 is then the generic fact that the gradient flow of a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex function contracts the squared distance to its minimizer at rate \(2\lambda\); Proof 2 is precisely that computation, \(\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\|h_t-1\|_\pi^2 = -\langle h_t-1,\nabla_\pi F(h_t)\rangle_\pi = -2F(h_t)\). This is why \(\chi^2\) is the natural convergence measure for the heat flow: it is the squared norm of the geometry in which the flow is a gradient flow.
Question for later. Is there a geometry in which the heat flow is the gradient flow of the entropy, with geodesic convexity of the entropy giving entropy decay? Yes: on \(\mathbb R^n\), Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (1998) with the Wasserstein-2 metric (convexity ↔︎ Bakry–Émery curvature); on finite Markov chains, Maas (2011) and Mielke (2011) with a discrete transport metric; Erbar–Maas then showed that a lower bound on the resulting entropic Ricci curvature implies a modified log-Sobolev inequality — the discrete analog of Bakry–Émery.
Discrete time. For the lazy chain, \(\operatorname{Var}_\pi(P_{\rm lazy}^th)\le(1-\lambda/2)^{2t}\operatorname{Var}_\pi(h)\), since \(P_{\rm lazy}\) has eigenvalues \(1-\lambda_k/2\in[0,1]\). For the non-lazy chain the factor is \(\lambda_\star^{2t}\) with \(\lambda_\star=\max_{k\ge2}|1-\lambda_k|\) — which is \(1\) on bipartite graphs.

5. What this implies for \(\ell_1\) and entropy

5.1 Two-sided bound on the mixing time
Theorem. For the continuous-time walk, with \(\pi_{\min}=\min_x\pi_x\), \[
\frac1\lambda\log\frac1{2\varepsilon}\ \le\ t_{\rm mix}(\varepsilon)\ \le\ \frac1\lambda\Big(\tfrac12\log\frac1{\pi_{\min}}+\log\frac1{2\varepsilon}\Big).
\]
Upper bound. By Lemma (1) and §4, \(\|\delta_xH_t-\pi\|_{TV}\le\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(\delta_xH_t\Vert\pi)}\le\frac12e^{-\lambda t}\sqrt{1/\pi_x}\). Set the right side \(\le\varepsilon\). \(\square\)
Lower bound. Let \(f=\varphi_2\) rescaled so \(\|f\|_\infty = 1 = |f(x)|\) for some \(x\). Then \(\mathbb E_\pi f = \langle f,\mathbf 1\rangle_\pi = 0\) and \((H_tf)(x) = e^{-\lambda t}f(x)\). For any \(\mu\), \(|\mathbb E_\mu f-\mathbb E_\pi f|\le\|\mu-\pi\|_1\|f\|_\infty = 2\|\mu-\pi\|_{TV}\). With \(\mu = \delta_xH_t\): \(e^{-\lambda t} = |(H_tf)(x)| \le 2\|\delta_xH_t-\pi\|_{TV}\). So \(d(t)\ge\frac12e^{-\lambda t}\). \(\square\)
Lazy discrete version (same proofs, \(e^{-\lambda}\to 1-\lambda/2\)): \((\tfrac2\lambda-1)\log\tfrac1{2\varepsilon}\le t_{\rm mix}(\varepsilon)\le\tfrac2\lambda\big(\tfrac12\log\tfrac1{\pi_{\min}}+\log\tfrac1{2\varepsilon}\big)\), using \(\log\frac1{1-x}\le\frac x{1-x}\) for the lower bound (cf. Levin–Peres–Wilmer, Ch. 12).
Reading. The gap determines \(t_{\rm mix}\) up to a factor \(\log(1/\pi_{\min})\approx\log n\). The loss comes entirely from the initial value \(\chi^2(\delta_x\Vert\pi)\approx n\): \(\chi^2\) needs time \(\approx\log(\chi^2_0)/(2\lambda)\) just to get below 1. Two ways to recover it, previewed in §5.3 and §6.5: use more of the spectrum than \(\lambda_2\), or measure with a distance whose initial value is smaller.


5.2 Entropy from the spectral gap
From Lemma (3): \(D(\mu_t\Vert\pi)\le\log\big(1+e^{-2\lambda t}\chi^2(\mu_0\Vert\pi)\big)\). Starting from \(\delta_x\) this is \(\approx\log(1/\pi_x) - 2\lambda t\) (useless) until \(t\approx\log(1/\pi_x)/(2\lambda)\), and \(\approx e^{-2\lambda t}/\pi_x\) afterwards. So the spectral gap gives exponential eventual decay of entropy at rate \(2\lambda\), but with the same \(\log(1/\pi_{\min})\) burn-in.


5.3 Preparing the ground for log-Sobolev inequalities
Redo Proof 2 of §4 with entropy. Since \(\mathbb E_\pi h_t\) is constant and \(L_{rw}\) is self-adjoint with \(L_{rw}\mathbf 1=0\): \[
\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Ent}_\pi(h_t) = \mathbb E_\pi\big[(1+\log h_t)\,\partial_th_t\big] = -\langle\log h_t,L_{rw}h_t\rangle_\pi = -\mathcal E(h_t,\log h_t)\ \le 0 .
\] \(\mathcal E(h,\log h)\) is the entropy production (discrete Fisher information). The functional inequality that closes the loop is the modified log-Sobolev inequality (MLSI) with constant \(\rho_0\): \[
\rho_0\operatorname{Ent}_\pi(h)\le\mathcal E(h,\log h)\quad\forall h>0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad D(\mu_t\Vert\pi)\le e^{-\rho_0t}D(\mu_0\Vert\pi).
\] Then Pinsker gives \(\|\delta_xH_t-\pi\|_{TV}\le\sqrt{\tfrac12e^{-\rho_0t}\log(1/\pi_x)}\), i.e., \[
t_{\rm mix}(\varepsilon)\le\frac1{\rho_0}\Big(\log\log\frac1{\pi_{\min}}+\log\frac1{2\varepsilon^2}\Big).
\] \(\log(1/\pi_{\min})\) has become \(\log\log(1/\pi_{\min})\) — because entropy starts at \(\log n\) instead of \(n\).
The price is the constant. Relations (both one-line proofs worth doing in class):

\(\rho_0\le2\lambda\). Linearize at equilibrium: \(h=1+\epsilon g\), \(\mathbb E_\pi g=0\). Then \(\operatorname{Ent}_\pi(h) = \frac{\epsilon^2}2\operatorname{Var}_\pi g+O(\epsilon^3)\) and \(\mathcal E(h,\log h) = \epsilon^2\mathcal E(g,g)+O(\epsilon^3)\), so MLSI forces \(\rho_0\le 2\mathcal E(g,g)/\operatorname{Var}_\pi g\) for every \(g\); take \(g=\varphi_2\).
Classical LSI. \(\alpha\operatorname{Ent}_\pi(f^2)\le\mathcal E(f,f)\) for all \(f\) (Gross; Diaconis–Saloff-Coste’s normalization). Since \((a-b)(\log a-\log b)\ge4(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\) (equivalent to \(\log(x/y)\ge 2\frac{x-y}{x+y}\)), we have \(\mathcal E(h,\log h)\ge4\mathcal E(\sqrt h,\sqrt h)\ge4\alpha\operatorname{Ent}_\pi(h)\), so \(\rho_0\ge4\alpha\). The same linearization gives \(\alpha\le\lambda/2\).

So \(4\alpha\le\rho_0\le2\lambda\). Whenever the log-Sobolev constant is comparable to the gap, entropy methods win by trading \(\log n\) for \(\log\log n\). When it is much smaller, they lose. Which happens, and how to compute \(\alpha\), is a later lecture.

6. Examples: bounding the gap from both sides

6.1 Toolkit
Upper bounds — test functions. Any non-constant \(f\) gives \(\lambda\le\mathcal E(f,f)/\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)\). Choose \(f\) to vary slowly across a bottleneck.
Degree comparison. If \(d_{\min}\le d_i\le d_{\max}\), then \[
\frac{\lambda_2(L)}{d_{\max}}\le\lambda_2(L_{rw})\le\frac{\lambda_2(L)}{d_{\min}},
\] because both are \(\min_f \frac{f^\top Lf}{\min_c\|f-c\|^2_m}\) with \(m=d\) resp. \(m=\mathbf 1\), and \(d_{\min}\|g\|^2\le\|g\|_d^2\le d_{\max}\|g\|^2\). All our examples have degrees in \([1,4]\), so we can work with the unnormalized \(L\) and convert at the end.
Lower bounds — canonical paths. This is the discrete version of the textbook proof of the 1-D Poincaré inequality: write \(f(b)-f(a) = \int_a^b f'\) and apply Cauchy–Schwarz. On a graph, choose for every ordered pair \((a,b)\), \(a\ne b\), a path \(\gamma_{ab}\) from \(a\) to \(b\), and choose edge lengths \(\ell_e>0\) (default: \(\ell\equiv1\)). Write \(\ell(\gamma)=\sum_{e\in\gamma}\ell_e\) and define the congestion \[
\kappa := \max_{e\in E}\ \frac{1}{w_e\,\ell_e}\sum_{(a,b):\,e\in\gamma_{ab}}\ell(\gamma_{ab}).
\]
Theorem (canonical paths; Jerrum–Sinclair, Diaconis–Stroock). \(\displaystyle\sum_{a,b\in V}(f_a-f_b)^2\le\kappa\,f^\top Lf\) for all \(f\); hence \(\lambda_2(L)\ge\dfrac{2n}{\kappa}\).
Proof. Telescoping along \(\gamma_{ab}\) and weighted Cauchy–Schwarz: \[
(f_b-f_a)^2 = \Big(\sum_{e\in\gamma_{ab}}\nabla_ef\Big)^2\le\Big(\sum_{e\in\gamma_{ab}}\ell_e\Big)\Big(\sum_{e\in\gamma_{ab}}\frac{(\nabla_ef)^2}{\ell_e}\Big).
\] Sum over ordered pairs and swap sums: \[
\sum_{a,b}(f_a-f_b)^2\le\sum_e w_e(\nabla_ef)^2\cdot\frac1{w_e\ell_e}\sum_{(a,b):e\in\gamma_{ab}}\ell(\gamma_{ab})
\] \[
\le\kappa\sum_ew_e(\nabla_ef)^2 = \kappa\,f^\top Lf .
\] Finally \(\sum_{a,b}(f_a-f_b)^2 = 2n\|f-\bar f\|^2\), so \(f^\top Lf\ge\frac{2n}{\kappa}\|f-\bar f\|^2\). \(\square\)
\(\pi\)-weighted version (for non-regular graphs, directly for \(\lambda\)): since \(\operatorname{Var}_\pi f = \frac12\sum_{a,b}\pi_a\pi_b(f_a-f_b)^2\) and \(\mathcal E(f,f) = \sum_eQ(e)(\nabla_ef)^2\) with \(Q(e) = \pi_iP_{ij} = w_e/\mathrm{vol}(V)\), the same proof gives \[
\lambda\ge\frac1{\kappa_\pi},\qquad\kappa_\pi = \max_e\frac{1}{Q(e)\ell_e}\cdot\frac12\sum_{(a,b):e\in\gamma_{ab}}\pi_a\pi_b\,\ell(\gamma_{ab}).
\] Interpretation. \(\kappa\) is the cost of routing a unit of “demand” between every pair simultaneously (a multicommodity flow, here unsplittable). If some edge set is a bottleneck, every routing congests it — so canonical paths certify the absence of bottlenecks, the dual of the test-function certificate. (This is the flow/cut duality behind Cheeger next week and Leighton–Rao later.)


6.2 The cycle \(C_n\)
Exact. \(L\) is circulant; \(f_j(x) = e^{2\pi\mathrm i jx/n}\) gives \((Lf_j)(x) = (2-e^{2\pi\mathrm ij/n}-e^{-2\pi\mathrm ij/n})f_j(x)\), so the eigenvalues are \(2-2\cos(2\pi j/n)\), \(j=0,\dots,n-1\) (real eigenvectors: cos and sin). Since \(D=2I\), \[
\lambda = 1-\cos\frac{2\pi}n = 2\sin^2\frac\pi n\approx\frac{2\pi^2}{n^2}.
\] Test function (upper bound without Fourier): \(f(x) = \cos(2\pi x/n)\) is exact; even the “tent” \(f(x) = \min(x,n-x)-\text{mean}\) gives \(\lambda\le O(1/n^2)\).
Canonical paths (\(n=2m+1\) odd, shortest paths, which are unique; \(\ell\equiv1\)). For each vertex there are 2 vertices at each distance \(1,\dots,m\), so \(\sum_{(a,b)}|\gamma_{ab}|^2 = 2n\sum_{s=1}^m s^2\). By rotation symmetry every edge carries the same load, and \(\sum_e(\text{load of }e) = \sum_{(a,b)}|\gamma_{ab}|^2\), so \[
\kappa = \frac{2n\sum_{s\le m}s^2}{n} = \frac{m(m+1)(2m+1)}3 = \frac{n(n^2-1)}{12}
\] \[
\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda_2(L)\ge\frac{24}{n^2-1},\quad\lambda = \tfrac12\lambda_2(L)\ge\frac{12}{n^2-1}.
\] Compare \(2\pi^2\approx19.7\): canonical paths get the right order with constant \(12\) vs \(19.7\).


6.3 The \(k\times k\) grid (\(n=k^2\))
Exact (optional). \(L(G\,\square\,H) = L_G\otimes I+I\otimes L_H\), so \(\operatorname{spec}L(P_k\square P_k) = \{\mu_i+\mu_j\}\) with \(\mu_j = 2-2\cos(\pi j/k)\) the path eigenvalues (eigenvectors \(\cos(\pi j(x-\frac12)/k)\) — the Neumann cosines). Hence \(\lambda_2(L) = 2-2\cos(\pi/k)\approx\pi^2/k^2\). (The normalized \(L_{rw}\) does not tensorize exactly because boundary degrees differ; use degree comparison, \(2\le d\le4\).)
Test function. \(f(x,y) = x-\frac{k+1}2\) (coordinates \(1..k\)): \(f^\top Lf = k(k-1)\) (only horizontal edges, each difference 1), \(\|f\|^2 = k\cdot\frac{k(k^2-1)}{12}\), so \(\lambda_2(L)\le\frac{12}{k(k+1)}\). With \(d_{\min}=2\): \(\lambda\le\frac{6}{k(k+1)}\).
Canonical paths: “L-shaped” routing — from \(a=(a_x,a_y)\) go horizontally along row \(a_y\) to column \(b_x\), then vertically to \(b\). Lengths \(\le2(k-1)\). - Horizontal edge in row \(r\) between columns \(c,c+1\): used by \((a,b)\) iff \(a\) is in row \(r\) and \(a_x,b_x\) are on opposite sides. Count: \(2\cdot c(k-c)\cdot k\le k^3/2\). - Vertical edge in column \(c\) between rows \(r,r+1\): used iff \(b\) is in column \(c\) and \(a_y,b_y\) on opposite sides; \(a_x\) arbitrary. Count: \(2\cdot r(k-r)\cdot k\le k^3/2\).
So \(\kappa\le\frac{k^3}2\cdot2(k-1) = k^3(k-1)\) and \(\lambda_2(L)\ge\frac{2k^2}{k^3(k-1)} = \frac2{k(k-1)}\); with \(d_{\max}=4\), \(\lambda\ge\frac1{2k(k-1)}\). Together: \(\lambda = \Theta(1/k^2) = \Theta(1/n)\).


6.4 The complete binary tree (depth \(h\), \(n = 2^{h+1}-1\))
Test function (bottleneck at the root). \(f=+1\) on the left subtree, \(-1\) on the right, \(0\) at the root. By symmetry \(\mathbb E_\pi f=0\); only the two root edges see a difference, so \(\sum w(\nabla f)^2 = 2\); and \(\sum_id_if_i^2 = \mathrm{vol}(V)-d_{\rm root} = 2(n-1)-2\). Hence \[
\lambda\le\frac{2}{2n-4} = \frac1{n-2}.
\] Canonical paths, unit lengths. Paths in a tree are forced. An edge whose lower endpoint is at depth \(j\) cuts off a subtree of size \(s_j = 2^{h-j+1}-1\); it is used by \(2s_j(n-s_j)\le n^2/2\) ordered pairs, each of length \(\le2h\). So \(\kappa\le n^2h\) and \(\lambda_2(L)\ge\frac2{nh}\) — off by a factor \(h\approx\log_2n\). The culprit: Cauchy–Schwarz with \(\ell\equiv1\) charges every edge of a long path equally, but only the top edges are congested.
Canonical paths, weighted lengths. Put \(\ell_e = 2^{-j/2}\) on depth-\(j\) edges (cheap where congested). Then \(\ell(\gamma)\le2\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j/2} = 2(\sqrt2+1)\), and using \(s_j<(n+1)2^{-j}\), \[
\frac1{\ell_e}\sum_{\gamma\ni e}\ell(\gamma)\le2^{j/2}\cdot2s_jn\cdot2(\sqrt2+1)
\] \[
<4(\sqrt2+1)\,n(n+1)\,2^{-j/2}\le2(2+\sqrt2)\,n(n+1).
\] So \(\kappa<2(2+\sqrt2)n(n+1)\) and \(\lambda_2(L)>\frac1{(2+\sqrt2)(n+1)}\); with \(d_{\max}=3\), \(\lambda>\frac1{3(2+\sqrt2)(n+1)}\). Together: \(\lambda = \Theta(1/n)\).
Moral: the choice of lengths \(\ell\) is the discrete analog of choosing a weight in a weighted Poincaré/Hardy inequality; with the right choice, paths are tight up to constants here.

Discussion points.

The lower bound \(t_{\rm rel}\) is tight on all three graphs; the generic \(\chi^2\) upper bound loses exactly \(\log n\).
The loss is not in \(\chi^2\) as a distance — it’s in using only \(\lambda_2\). By the spectral formula, \(\chi^2(\delta_xH_t\Vert\pi) = \sum_{k\ge2}e^{-2\lambda_kt}\varphi_k(x)^2\), and \(\sum_k\varphi_k(x)^2 = 1/\pi_x\). On a vertex-transitive graph each eigenspace contributes equally at every vertex, so \(\chi^2(\delta_xH_t\Vert\pi) = \sum_{k\ge2}e^{-2\lambda_kt}\) exactly. For the cycle, \(1-\cos\theta\ge2\theta^2/\pi^2\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\) gives \(\chi^2\le2\sum_{j\ge1}e^{-16tj^2/n^2}\), which is \(O(1)\) at \(t = \Theta(n^2)\): the \(\ell^2\) mixing time is \(\Theta(n^2)\), not \(n^2\log n\). The generic bound pretends all \(n-1\) modes decay as slowly as the slowest one.
When even \(t_{\rm rel}\) is not tight: the hypercube. Continuous-time walk on \(\{0,1\}^d\) (flip a uniform coordinate at rate 1): eigenvalues \(2|S|/d\), \(S\subseteq[d]\), so \(t_{\rm rel}=d/2\), and exactly \(\chi^2(t) = (1+e^{-4t/d})^d-1\), which drops below a constant at \(t\approx\frac d4\log d\); TV has cutoff at the same time (Diaconis; LPW). Here \(\log(1/\pi_{\min}) = d\log2\): the \(\chi^2\)-from-gap bound gives \(\Theta(d^2)\), the gap lower bound gives \(\Theta(d)\), the truth is \(\Theta(d\log d)\). The log-Sobolev constant of the hypercube is \(\Theta(1/d)\) (tensorization of the two-point LSI), so §5.3 gives \(\Theta(d\cdot\log\log 2^d) = \Theta(d\log d)\) — tight. This is the motivating example for LSIs.
Bipartiteness: all three graphs (and the hypercube) are bipartite — the non-lazy discrete walk never mixes; continuous time or laziness is not a technicality.
